articles.title: Nvidia shares slide as Trump's role in Jensen Huang's comeback questioned by US politicians
articles.summary: Nvidia's stock market value surged on the annoucement of Huang's reappointment, but some of the gains reversed in Tuesday trading.
articles.content:
Shares in Nvidia dipped on Tuesday as US politicans questioned President Donald Trump's role in the return of Jensen Huang as chief executive.

Huang was handed back his job at the AI microchip maker on Monday less than two weeks after he was forced to resign following the revelations of extra marital affairs, one of which was with a suspected Chinese spy.

Trump has said he played a big role in the 63-year-old's reinstatment, which has led to questions and backlash from US lawmakers.

While Nvidia's stock market value surged on the annoucement of Huang's reappointment, some of the gains were reversed in volatile Tuesday trading.

The company's share price was down almost 8% on Tuesday, but remained well above the level it closed at on Friday, before Huang's shock return was revealed.

However, Nvidia was not the only semiconductor chip company to experience share price declines on Tuesday, with rival AMD down more than 10%.

Broadcom and Marvell Technology shares were also lower, suggesting that investors were continuing to weigh up concerns over potential regulation by newly-elected Democrats, as well as the central question as to whether the huge amounts being invested in AI will pay off.

Nvidia's share price for example, is down almost 30% over the past six months and had been on the decline before the scandal involving its co-founder emerged earlier this month.

The company's board reinstated Huang on Monday in a shock U-turn on its original position. Harvey Jones, chairman of Nvidia's board, said Huang's return was in the "best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers".

The board said it had received input from senior levels of the US government and was confident that Huang's reinstatement posed no national security risk.

Trump said he had spoken to the company's directors and convinced them to bring back Huang.

"They did ask for assurance on the national security threat," Trump told CNBC. "And we gave them assurances at least with everything we know. And we know a lot."

Republican representative Don Bacon said Nvidia should have "ignored the Administration's inexplicable desire to save Huang", while Republican senator Pete Ricketts said Huang's behaviour "doesn't absolve Nvidia of answering for national security concerns and unaccounted-for chips".

Democratic representative Robert Garcia, the incoming chairman of the House oversight committee, said Trump's "direct involvement" with Nvidia's decision "raises serious national security and corruption questions", and Democratic senator Ruben Gallego said Congress needed to "investigate what stock positions took place before the announcement".

Huang is still set to appear before Congress next week, where the Nvidia boss will be questioned over his relationship with Alice Huang, alleged to be a spy for China, due to national security concerns.

The US Commerce Department announced it was preparing to blacklist Megaspeed, the Singapore-based Nvidia customer where Alice Huang (no relation) was chief executive. China has denied the spying allegations.

articles.title: Nine delectable Thanksgiving sides – from a ‘perfect’ gravy to Ottolenghi’s stuffing biscuits

articles.content:

L et’s be honest, side dishes are the true workhorses of Thanksgiving dinner. From a classic green been casserole perfected by Hetty Lui McKinnon to Yotam Ottolenghi’s twist on stuffing, here are nine of our go-to trimmings for Thanksgiving dinner. Or explore more from our huge collection .

Rukmini Iyer’s jewelled winter salad adds a burst of color to any spread. Iyer recommends roasting the squash the day before and marinating the beans overnight.

1 small butternut squash , peeled, deseeded and cut into 2/3 in cubes 5 tbsp olive oil 2 tsp ras el hanout 1 tsp sea salt flakes 2 small red onions (or 1 large one), peeled and each cut into eight equal wedges Juice of 1 lemon , plus 3 strips of zest (use a speed peeler) 3 garlic cloves , peeled and finely sliced 20 oz canned butter beans, drained and rinsed 1 oz flat-leaf parsley , roughly chopped 1 oz cilantro , roughly chopped 1 1/2 cups feta , cut into 1/2 in cubes Seeds from 1 pomegranate 1/2 cup pistachios , roughly chopped (if you can find the bright-green Sicilian ones, so much the better)

Heat the oven to 390F. Mix the squash, two tablespoons of olive oil, the ras el hanout and salt in a roasting tray large enough to hold everything in a single layer. In a small bowl, toss the onion wedges with half the lemon juice (this will help them keep their colour), add them to the squash tray, then roast for 30 minutes.

Meanwhile, put the remaining oil, the garlic and lemon zest in a large frying pan over a low heat, and warm through for two to three minutes without letting the garlic brown. Add the butter beans, cook, stirring occasionally, for six to seven minutes, then take off the heat.

Once the squash is ready, gently stir the butter beans and herbs into the tray, then dress with the remaining lemon juice. Taste and adjust the salt as needed, then top with the feta, pomegranate and pistachios, and serve warm or at room temperature.

A fresh, crunchy slaw from Yotam Ottolenghi to brighten up a heavy meal. Bonus: It can be made in advance – just don’t add the dressing until you’re sitting down to eat.

2/3 oz sunflower seeds 1 tbsp maple syrup 1/3 cup olive oil 1 tsp nigella seeds , lightly crushed in a mortar 2 kohlrabi , peeled and cut into matchsticks 2 carrots , peeled, halved lengthways and thinly sliced 2/3 oz parsley , roughly chopped, plus 1 tbsp extra to serve 2/3 cup Greek yoghurt 2/3 oz fresh horseradish , peeled and finely grated (or good-quality creamed horseradish) 1 tbsp lemon juice Fine sea salt and freshly ground black pepper

Put the sunflower seeds, maple syrup and two tablespoons of oil in a small pan on a medium-high heat and cook, stirring occasionally, for two minutes, until the sunflower seeds start to brown. Take the pan off the heat, stir in the nigella seeds and a quarter-teaspoon of salt, then pour into a heatproof sieve set over a bowl. Once the solids are cool enough to handle, break up the seeds with your hands, then return them to the oil, to finish the crunchy sunflower seed topping.

Put the kohlrabi, carrots, and parsley in a large bowl and toss to combine.

In a medium bowl, mix the remaining three tablespoons oil with the yoghurt, horseradish, lemon juice, three-quarters of a teaspoon of salt and a good grind of pepper.

Just before serving, pour the dressing over the kohlrabi mixture and toss to coat. Transfer half the slaw to a wide bowl, spoon over half the sunflower seed topping, then repeat with the remaining slaw and sunflower seed topping. Scatter over the extra parsley and serve.

Hetty Lui McKinnon’s lighter twist on a classic, this time with shiitake mushrooms, tahini and homemade crispy turmeric shallots.

3 1/2 oz black lentils, rinsed Extra-virgin olive oil 2 and 1/4 lbs green beans, trimmed and halved 3 cups fresh shiitake mushrooms, coarsely chopped or sliced 2 thyme sprigs, leaves picked 1⁄3 cup tahini Juice of 1⁄2 lemon 1 garlic clove , very finely chopped Handful of chopped chives Sea salt and black pepper

2 French shallots , finely sliced into rounds 2 tbsp rice flour 1 tsp ground turmeric 1⁄2 cup sunflower or other high-temperature oil , plus extra if needed Sea salt and black pepper

Substitute Shiitake mushrooms: button or Swiss brown mushrooms French shallots: small red onions Rice flour: plain flour

Bring a pot of salted water to the boil. Add the lentils, cover and cook for 15-20 minutes, until the lentils are just tender. Drain.

Meanwhile, make the crispy turmeric shallots. Toss the shallot rounds together with the rice flour, turmeric and a pinch of salt and pepper, using your hands to break up the rings so that they are evenly coated.

Heat the oil in a small saucepan until very hot (test with a wooden chopstick or wooden spoon; if it sizzles, the oil is ready). Add the shallot rings to the oil a handful at a time and fry until golden brown. When ready, place them on a paper towel to absorb excess oil and immediately sprinkle with some sea salt. Repeat until all the shallot rings are cooked. Allow to cool.

Heat a splash of olive oil in a large frying pan and add the beans. Season with sea salt and black pepper and cook for 5–7 minutes, until the beans are tender and turning golden. Remove from the pan and set aside. In the same pan, add another drizzle of oil along with the mushrooms and thyme and cook until the mushrooms have turned golden. Remove from the heat.

Place the tahini in a small bowl, add the lemon juice, garlic and chives and slowly whisk in cold water, one tablespoon at a time, until the mixture is the consistency of thickened cream. Season with sea salt and lots of black pepper.

Combine the beans with the mushrooms, lentils and tahini sauce. Transfer to the baking dish and bake for 10-12 minutes. Take the dish out of the oven, top with the crispy turmeric shallots and return to the oven for another five minutes. Serve immediately.

The crispy turmeric shallots can be made up to a day ahead. If you are short on time, buy ready-made crispy fried shallots from your Asian grocery store or supermarket.

The green bean casserole can be made the day ahead and topped and baked with the onions just before eating.

Ottolenghi’s stuffing-inspired biscuits infuse onion, garlic, rosemary and celery salt into a handheld treat. He suggests eating them fresh out of the oven, “though any leftovers will still be great the next day, gently warmed through, sliced open and packed with more butter, and any cold meat and cheese.”

For the onion mix 1/4 stick (2 1/4tbsp) unsalted butter 1 onion , peeled and finely chopped (150g) 1 garlic clove , peeled and crushed 1/4 oz rosemary leaves (about 1 tsp), finely chopped 1/3 oz sage leaves (about ¾ tsp), finely chopped ½ tsp celery salt 2 tbsp runny honey

For the biscuit dough 3/4 cup buttermilk 1 egg 2 cups all-purpose flour , plus extra for dusting 2½ tsp baking powder ¼ tsp baking soda Fine sea salt 1 stick (1/2 cup) fridge-cold unsalted butter , cut into 3/4 in cubes 3 1/2 oz onion mix (see above and method) 1 cup mature cheddar , coarsely grated, plus 3/4tbsp extra for sprinkling

Melt the butter for the onion mix in a medium frying pan, then stir in all the remaining onion mix ingredients apart from the honey and cook, stirring every now and then, for 10 minutes, until soft but not coloured. Take off the heat, stir in the honey and leave to cool completely.

For the biscuits, whisk the buttermilk and egg in a bowl, then put in the fridge to cool. Put the flour, baking powder, bicarb and a half teaspoon of fine salt into a food processor and pulse to combine. Add the cubed cold butter and pulse until it’s broken down into pea-sized pieces.

Set aside a tablespoon of the buttermilk-egg mix, then pour the rest into the food processor and pulse until the dough is crumbly but not quite coming together. Add the cooled onion mix and the grated cheddar, then pulse again a couple of times just to combine.

Try this recipe and many more on the new Feast app: scan or click here for your free trial.

Tip out the dough on to a lightly floured surface and, with well-floured hands, gently compress into a rough square. Fold this in half, then compress again into a square. Fold it in half again, this time the other way, then compress into a square once again: the square should by now be about 8 in wide and 1-1/4 in thick. Cut the dough into nine even squares and arrange these on a large baking tray lined with greaseproof paper. Brush the tops with the reserved tablespoon of buttermilk-egg mix, then sprinkle over the final 3-1/4tbsp cheddar. Put in the fridge for 20 minutes to cool (or cover and freeze until required).

Heat the oven to 415F. Take the biscuits out of the fridge (or freezer) and bake for 25 minutes (30 minutes if baking from frozen), rotating the tray once halfway through, until nicely browned.

Take the tray out of the oven, transfer the biscuits to a rack, leave to cool for 10 minutes, then serve at once.

“Vegetarians tend to be sadly ill-served in the gravy department,” writes Felicity Cloake. Fortunately there’s this meat-free version – which gets its umami flavor from dried porcini mushrooms. Even better? Because it’s not reliant on the turkey, it can be made in advance.

2 tbsp oil 2 onions , peeled and roughly chopped 2 carrots , roughly chopped 2 celery sticks , roughly chopped (use the leaves, too, assuming there are any) 1 bay leaf 1 sprig fresh thyme 1/4 cup dried porcini 2 tbsp plain flour or cornflour 3/4 cup white wine (optional) 2 tsp Marmite or other yeast product (optional) Port and/or madeira, sweet sherry, redcurrant jelly, cranberry sauce, etc, to taste

Heat the oil in a medium saucepan over a medium-low heat, add the chopped vegetables and herbs, and fry, stirring regularly to ensure they don’t catch and burn, for about 15 minutes, until soft and golden.

Meanwhile, whiz the mushrooms to a fine powder in a food processor (or pound them in a mortar), then mix with 1/2 cup of warm water.

Once the vegetables are done, stir in the flour, cook for a minute or so longer, then, scraping the bottom of the pan as you do so, stir in the wine, 2 cups of water (or 3 cups of water if not using wine) and the mushroom paste. Bring to a simmer, stirring until thickened, then pass through a sieve and discard the vegetables and herbs.

Return the gravy to the pan, bring to a simmer, then stir in the Marmite, if using. Add the port or similar to taste; season and serve.

Meera Sodha’s crisp roast cauliflower and pilaf works both as a centerpiece and a “showstopping” side dish. Seasoned with chilli and fresh cilantro, most of the dish can be made ahead.

For the cauliflower 2 tsp ground cumin ½ tsp kashmiri chilli powder ½ tsp fine sea salt 2 tbsp canola oil 1 large cauliflower (or 2 small ones), leaves removed ( 1-3/4 lbs )

For the pilaf 1 1/2 cups basmati rice 1/4 cup canola oil 2 onions , peeled and sliced 1 tsp fine sea salt 1 tsp ground cumin 1 tsp ground coriander ¼ tsp ground black pepper 1 3/4 oz shelled unsalted pistachios 1 3/4 oz whole almonds , roughly chopped in half 2/3 oz fresh cilantro , finely chopped 2/3 oz fresh parsley , finely chopped

For the tahini sauce 1/3 cup tahini 3 tbsp canola oil 1 lemon , juiced to get 2 tbsp ½ small garlic clove , peeled and grated 1/4 tsp fine sea salt, plus more to taste

Heat the oven to 390F. In a small bowl, mix the cumin, chilli powder, half a teaspoon of salt and two tablespoons of oil until you have a smooth paste.

Cut the base of the core off the cauliflower, so it stands flat. Rub the whole cauliflower all over with the spice paste, then put it in a high-sided or lipped baking tray. Pour 1/2 cup warm water around the cauliflower, roast for an hour, until golden on top and tender inside (check by prodding with a skewer or cake tester), then remove and set aside.

While the cauliflower is roasting, wash the rice really well in a sieve, until the water runs clear, then put in a bowl, pour over warm water to cover and leave to soak until needed.

Put 1/4 cup of oil in a large saucepan with a tight-fitting lid, turn on the heat to medium, then saute the onions with a teaspoon of salt, stirring occasionally, for 12 minutes, until soft and dark.

Add the spices, cook for a minute, then add the nuts and stir to coat. Drain the rice well, then add to the onions, give everything one more stir to distribute the nuts and onions through the rice, then add 2 cups just-boiled water and clap on the lid. Bring to a boil, cook for a couple of minutes, then turn down to the lowest heat and cook for 12 minutes. Take off the heat and leave to steam and settle for 10 minutes – do not lift the lid.

While the rice settles, make the tahini sauce. Put everything in a jam jar or similar, add four tablespoons of cold water, then shake like a person possessed until you have an emulsified sauce: it should be like double cream and pourable; if it is too thick, add a smidge more water; too thin, more tahini paste. Check the seasoning and adjust the salt and lemon juice as necessary.

To serve, stir the chopped herbs through the rice, then tip out on to your best platter and top with the cauliflower head. Pour the tahini sauce into a pretty jug. Stick a sharp knife in the cauliflower and encourage guests to help themselves to rice, a wedge of cauliflower and a healthy pouring of tahini sauce.

Ottolenghi’s “sticky, salty, nutty and delicious” roasted brussels sprouts – adorned with pistachios and tarragon – are a sweet and savory dish.

1 1/2 lbs brussels sprouts , trimmed and halved lengthways 1/3 cup olive oil Fine sea salt and black pepper 1 3/4 oz peeled pistachios , lightly crushed in a mortar 2 oranges , zest finely grated, to get 2 tsp, then juiced, to get 250ml 2 tbsp soy sauce 2 tbsp maple syrup 1/4oz tarragon leaves

Heat the oven to its highest setting – at least 475F. Toss the halved sprouts with the oil, half a teaspoon of salt and a good grind of pepper, then spread out on a large baking tray lined with greaseproof paper and roast for 10 minutes. Stir in the pistachios and roast for another 10 minutes, until the sprouts are nicely browned and the pistachios have toasted.

Meanwhile, put the orange zest and juice, soy sauce and maple syrup in a small saucepan on a medium-high heat, and leave to cook for five to eight minutes, until the sauce has reduced by three-quarters and has turned syrupy.

Once the sprouts are cooked, pour the syrup all over them, scatter over half the tarragon and toss to combine. Transfer to a platter, sprinkle over the remaining tarragon and serve.

After years of experimenting with mac and cheese recipes, Sodhi came up with this creamy, vegan cashew “cheese” dish, spiked with lime and chipotle.

5 2/3 oz shelled cashew nuts 1/3 cup nutritional yeast 1 tsp garlic granules 1 tsp onion granules 1 tsp dijon mustard 1 tbsp cider vinegar ¼ tsp smoked paprika ⅓ tsp turmeric Fine sea salt 10 1/2 oz macaroni Olive oil , to drizzle on the pasta

For the garlic and parsley oil 2 1/3 oz parsley , woody stems removed, the rest roughly chopped 2 garlic cloves , peeled and chopped 1/2 cup olive oil 2 tbsp lime juice ½ tsp chipotle chilli flakes ½ tsp fine sea salt

Put the cashews and 1 cup water in a medium-sized saucepan that’s big enough to cook the pasta in later. Bring to a boil, then turn down to a simmer and cook for eight minutes. Drain the nuts and discard the water.

While the cashews are cooking, make the garlic and parsley oil: put all the ingredients in a blender and blitz until very well chopped. Transfer to a small bowl and rinse out the blender.

Put the drained cashews into the blender, then add 2/3 cup cold water, the nutritional yeast, garlic granules, onion granules, mustard, vinegar, paprika, turmeric and a half teaspoon of salt and blend until very smooth.

In the same saucepan you boiled the cashews in, bring 2 quarts of water to a boil, add two teaspoons of salt, then cook the macaroni until al dente, according to the packet instructions. Near the end of the cooking time, scoop out a mugful of the starchy cooking water, then drain the pasta, return it to the pan and drizzle with a little oil.

Put the pasta back on a medium heat, add the “cheese” sauce, then stir and toss, adding the reserved pasta water a couple of tablespoons at a time – I ended up using 3/4 cup – until the sauce turns creamy and coats the pasta.

Divide the pasta between four plates or shallow bowls, spoon over the garlic and parsley oil, then serve.

Everyone likes to make stuffing their own, and this Ottolenghi version is infused with parsnips, pecorino and dried currants.

2 onions , peeled and thinly sliced 1 1/3 lbs parsnips , peeled, cut in half lengthways, then chopped into roughly 3/4 in pieces 3 celery sticks (200g), trimmed and chopped into roughly 1/2 in pieces (180g) 1/4 cup olive oil 1 1/2 tsp finely chopped thyme leaves Fine sea salt and black pepper 10 1/2 oz sourdough , cut into 3/4 in -thick slices 3 garlic cloves , peeled and crushed 1 1/4 cup pecorino , grated 1/2 cup heavy cream 1 2/3 cup chicken or vegetable stock 2 eggs 1/3 cup dried currants 4-5 spring onions ( 2oz ), trimmed and cut into 1cm pieces 2/3 oz parsley , finely chopped, plus 1 tbsp extra to finish 1 1/2 tsp caraway seeds , toasted

Heat the oven to 475F. Put the first five ingredients in a medium-large baking dish – ideally about 9 in by 13 in – add three-quarters of a teaspoon of salt and a good grind of pepper and toss to coat. Roast for 25-30 minutes, stirring once or twice, until golden and slightly charred, then remove from the oven and turn it down to 390F. Use a fork to smash up the parsnips.

Meanwhile, toast the bread on a low oven shelf for 10 minutes, until evenly golden and crunchy, then leave to cool and cut into roughly 1/4 in pieces.

Put the garlic, pecorino, cream, stock and eggs in a large bowl, add a half teaspoon of salt and a good grind of black pepper, and whisk to combine. Add the parsnip mixture to the cream bowl, stir in the currants, spring onions, parsley and caraway, then set aside for five minutes, so the bread absorbs most of the liquid. Tip everything back into the baking dish and roast for 20-25 minutes, until golden on top. Serve hot.

He suggests eating them fresh out of the oven, “though any leftovers will still be great the next day, gently warmed through, sliced open and packed with more butter, and any cold meat and cheese.”

For the onion mix 1/4 stick (2 1/4tbsp) unsalted butter 1 onion , peeled and finely chopped (150g) 1 garlic clove , peeled and crushed 1/4 oz rosemary leaves (about 1 tsp), finely chopped 1/3 oz sage leaves (about ¾ tsp), finely chopped ½ tsp celery salt 2 tbsp runny honey

For the biscuit dough 3/4 cup buttermilk 1 egg 2 cups all-purpose flour , plus extra for dusting 2½ tsp baking powder ¼ tsp baking soda Fine sea salt 1 stick (1/2 cup) fridge-cold unsalted butter , cut into 3/4 in cubes 3 1/2 oz onion mix (see above and method) 1 cup mature cheddar , coarsely grated, plus 3/4tbsp extra for sprinkling

Melt the butter for the onion mix in a medium frying pan, then stir in all the remaining onion mix ingredients apart from the honey and cook, stirring every now and then, for 10 minutes, until soft but not coloured. Take off the heat, stir in the honey and leave to cool completely.

For the biscuits, whisk the buttermilk and egg in a bowl, then put in the fridge to cool. Put the flour, baking powder, bicarb and a half teaspoon of fine salt into a food processor and pulse to combine. Add the cubed cold butter and pulse until it’s broken down into pea-sized pieces.

Set aside a tablespoon of the buttermilk-egg mix, then pour the rest into the food processor and pulse until the dough is crumbly but not quite coming together. Add the cooled onion mix and the grated cheddar, then pulse again a couple of times just to combine.
Try this recipe and many more on the new Feast app: scan or click here for your free trial.

Tip out the dough on to a lightly floured surface and, with well-floured hands, gently compress into a rough square. Fold this in half, then compress again into a square. Fold it in half again, this time the other way, then compress into a square once again: the square should by now be about 8 in wide and 1-1/4 in thick. Cut the dough into nine even squares and arrange these on a large baking tray lined with greaseproof paper. Brush the tops with the reserved tablespoon of buttermilk-egg mix, then sprinkle over the final 3-1/4tbsp cheddar. Put in the fridge for 20 minutes to cool (or cover and freeze until required).
Heat the oven to 415F. Take the biscuits out of the fridge (or freezer) and bake for 25 minutes (30 minutes if baking from frozen), rotating the tray once halfway through, until nicely browned.
Take the tray out of the oven, transfer the biscuits to a rack, leave to cool for 10 minutes, then serve at once.

“Vegetarians tend to be sadly ill-served in the gravy department,” writes Felicity Cloake. Fortunately there’s this meat-free version – which gets its umami flavor from dried porcini mushrooms. Even better? Because it’s not reliant on the turkey, it can be made in advance.

2 tbsp oil 2 onions , peeled and roughly chopped 2 carrots , roughly chopped 2 celery sticks , roughly chopped (use the leaves, too, assuming there are any) 1 bay leaf 1 sprig fresh thyme 1/4 cup dried porcini 2 tbsp plain flour or cornflour 3/4 cup white wine (optional) 2 tsp Marmite or other yeast product (optional) Port and/or madeira, sweet sherry, redcurrant jelly, cranberry sauce, etc, to taste

Heat the oil in a medium saucepan over a medium-low heat, add the chopped vegetables and herbs, and fry, stirring regularly to ensure they don’t catch and burn, for about 15 minutes, until soft and golden.
Meanwhile, whiz the mushrooms to a fine powder in a food processor (or pound them in a mortar), then mix with 1/2 cup of warm water.

Once the vegetables are done, stir in the flour, cook for a minute or so longer, then, scraping the bottom of the pan as you do so, stir in the wine, 2 cups of water (or 3 cups of water if not using wine) and the mushroom paste. Bring to a simmer, stirring until thickened, then pass through a sieve and discard the vegetables and herbs.
Return the gravy to the pan, bring to a simmer, then stir in the Marmite, if using. Add the port or similar to taste; season and serve.
Meera Sodha’s crisp roast cauliflower and pilaf works both as a centerpiece and a “showstopping” side dish. Seasoned with chilli and fresh cilantro, most of the dish can be made ahead.
For the cauliflower 2 tsp ground cumin ½ tsp kashmiri chilli powder ½ tsp fine sea salt 2 tbsp canola oil 1 large cauliflower (or 2 small ones), leaves removed ( 1-3/4 lbs )

For the pilaf 1 1/2 cups basmati rice 1/4 cup canola oil 2 onions , peeled and sliced 1 tsp fine sea salt 1 tsp ground cumin 1 tsp ground coriander ¼ tsp ground black pepper 1 3/4 oz shelled unsalted pistachios 1 3/4 oz whole almonds , roughly chopped in half 2/3 oz fresh cilantro , finely chopped 2/3 oz fresh parsley , finely chopped
For the tahini sauce 1/3 cup tahini 3 tbsp canola oil 1 lemon , juiced to get 2 tbsp ½ small garlic clove , peeled and grated 1/4 tsp fine sea salt, plus more to taste
Heat the oven to 390F. In a small bowl, mix the cumin, chilli powder, half a teaspoon of salt and two tablespoons of oil until you have a smooth paste.

Cut the base of the core off the cauliflower, so it stands flat. Rub the whole cauliflower all over with the spice paste, then put it in a high-sided or lipped baking tray. Pour 1/2 cup warm water around the cauliflower, roast for an hour, until golden on top and tender inside (check by prodding with a skewer or cake tester), then remove and set aside.
While the cauliflower is roasting, wash the rice really well in a sieve, until the water runs clear, then put in a bowl, pour over warm water to cover and leave to soak until needed.
Put 1/4 cup of oil in a large saucepan with a tight-fitting lid, turn on the heat to medium, then saute the onions with a teaspoon of salt, stirring occasionally, for 12 minutes, until soft and dark.

Add the spices, cook for a minute, then add the nuts and stir to coat. Drain the rice well, then add to the onions, give everything one more stir to distribute the nuts and onions through the rice, then add 2 cups just-boiled water and clap on the lid. Bring to a boil, cook for a couple of minutes, then turn down to the lowest heat and cook for 12 minutes. Take off the heat and leave to steam and settle for 10 minutes – do not lift the lid.

While the rice settles, make the tahini sauce. Put everything in a jam jar or similar, add four tablespoons of cold water, then shake like a person possessed until you have an emulsified sauce: it should be like double cream and pourable; if it is too thick, add a smidge more water; too thin, more tahini paste. Check the seasoning and adjust the salt and lemon juice as necessary.

To serve, stir the chopped herbs through the rice, then tip out on to your best platter and top with the cauliflower head. Pour the tahini sauce into a pretty jug. Stick a sharp knife in the cauliflower and encourage guests to help themselves to rice, a wedge of cauliflower and a healthy pouring of tahini sauce.
Ottolenghi’s “sticky, salty, nutty and delicious” roasted brussels sprouts – adorned with pistachios and tarragon – are a sweet and savory dish.

1 1/2 lbs brussels sprouts , trimmed and halved lengthways 1/3 cup olive oil Fine sea salt and black pepper 1 3/4 oz peeled pistachios , lightly crushed in a mortar 2 oranges , zest finely grated, to get 2 tsp, then juiced, to get 250ml 2 tbsp soy sauce 2 tbsp maple syrup 1/4oz tarragon leaves

Heat the oven to its highest setting – at least 475F. Toss the halved sprouts with the oil, half a teaspoon of salt and a good grind of pepper, then spread out on a large baking tray lined with greaseproof paper and roast for 10 minutes. Stir in the pistachios and roast for another 10 minutes, until the sprouts are nicely browned and the pistachios have toasted.

Meanwhile, put the orange zest and juice, soy sauce and maple syrup in a small saucepan on a medium-high heat, and leave to cook for five to eight minutes, until the sauce has reduced by three-quarters and has turned syrupy.
Once the sprouts are cooked, pour the syrup all over them, scatter over half the tarragon and toss to combine. Transfer to a platter, sprinkle over the remaining tarragon and serve.
After years of experimenting with mac and cheese recipes, Sodhi came up with this creamy, vegan cashew “cheese” dish, spiked with lime and chipotle.

5 2/3 oz shelled cashew nuts 1/3 cup nutritional yeast 1 tsp garlic granules 1 tsp onion granules 1 tsp dijon mustard 1 tbsp cider vinegar ¼ tsp smoked paprika ⅓ tsp turmeric Fine sea salt 10 1/2 oz macaroni Olive oil , to drizzle on the pasta

For the garlic and parsley oil 2 1/3 oz parsley , woody stems removed, the rest roughly chopped 2 garlic cloves , peeled and chopped 1/2 cup olive oil 2 tbsp lime juice ½ tsp chipotle chilli flakes ½ tsp fine sea salt

Put the cashews and 1 cup water in a medium-sized saucepan that’s big enough to cook the pasta in later. Bring to a boil, then turn down to a simmer and cook for eight minutes. Drain the nuts and discard the water.
While the cashews are cooking, make the garlic and parsley oil: put all the ingredients in a blender and blitz until very well chopped. Transfer to a small bowl and rinse out the blender.

Put the drained cashews into the blender, then add 2/3 cup cold water, the nutritional yeast, garlic granules, onion granules, mustard, vinegar, paprika, turmeric and a half teaspoon of salt and blend until very smooth.

In the same saucepan you boiled the cashews in, bring 2 quarts of water to a boil, add two teaspoons of salt, then cook the macaroni until al dente, according to the packet instructions. Near the end of the cooking time, scoop out a mugful of the starchy cooking water, then drain the pasta, return it to the pan and drizzle with a little oil.

Put the pasta back on a medium heat, add the “cheese” sauce, then stir and toss, adding the reserved pasta water a couple of tablespoons at a time – I ended up using 3/4 cup – until the sauce turns creamy and coats the pasta.
Divide the pasta between four plates or shallow bowls, spoon over the garlic and parsley oil, then serve.
Everyone likes to make stuffing their own, and this Ottolenghi version is infused with parsnips, pecorino and dried currants.

2 onions , peeled and thinly sliced 1 1/3 lbs parsnips , peeled, cut in half lengthways, then chopped into roughly 3/4 in pieces 3 celery sticks (200g), trimmed and chopped into roughly 1/2 in pieces (180g) 1/4 cup olive oil 1 1/2 tsp finely chopped thyme leaves Fine sea salt and black pepper 10 1/2 oz sourdough , cut into 3/4 in -thick slices 3 garlic cloves , peeled and crushed 1 1/4 cup pecorino , grated 1/2 cup heavy cream 1 2/3 cup chicken or vegetable stock 2 eggs 1/3 cup dried currants 4-5 spring onions ( 2oz ), trimmed and cut into 1cm pieces 2/3 oz parsley , finely chopped, plus 1 tbsp extra to finish 1 1/2 tsp caraway seeds , toasted

Heat the oven to 475F. Put the first five ingredients in a medium-large baking dish – ideally about 9 in by 13 in – add three-quarters of a teaspoon of salt and a good grind of pepper and toss to coat. Roast for 25-30 minutes, stirring once or twice, until golden and slightly charred, then remove from the oven and turn it down to 390F. Use a fork to smash up the parsnips.
Meanwhile, toast the bread on a low oven shelf for 10 minutes, until evenly golden and crunchy, then leave to cool and cut into roughly 1/4 in pieces.

Put the garlic, pecorino, cream, stock and eggs in a large bowl, add a half teaspoon of salt and a good grind of black pepper, and whisk to combine. Add the parsnip mixture to the cream bowl, stir in the currants, spring onions, parsley and caraway, then set aside for five minutes, so the bread absorbs most of the liquid. Tip everything back into the baking dish and roast for 20-25 minutes, until golden on top. Serve hot.

articles.content:
A teen girl discovers she is a witch in this mostly magic-free reminder that original animation is stuck in an unoriginal place

A s bleak as Disney’s overreliance on sequels might have become, it’s not quite as bleak as the crumbling state of its original output. Obviously because of the former, the latter category has become that much less populated but even when the studio has recently bothered to release something without a number in the title, it’s been hard to really see the point.

With or without Pixar, films like Elio, Strange World, Raya and the Last Dragon, Luca, Elemental, Onward and Wish have all felt as uninspired as something a rival might try to desperately cobble together in an attempt to lure kids away from Disney. Three Thanksgivings ago, Wish was a particularly poor yet extremely smug example of how rubbishy things have got, a personality-free princess tale that doubled up as a 100-year anniversary victory lap. It was Disney’s worst-reviewed animated film in almost two decades and its deserved box office failure cost about $131m. Unperturbed, its co-director Fawn Veerasunthorn (along with Moana 2 director Jason Hand) is back this holiday with another rote rip-off adventure that doesn’t deserve its place in the kingdom.

In an attempt to conjure up that long-gone magic, Hexed is a film absolutely stuffed with it, a tale of witches, spells, cauldrons and curses that is at the very least neatly timed. Interest in all things Harry Potter remains sky-high (next month’s HBO adaptation is set to be the year’s most-watched TV show) as streaming hits like Carrie and The Body and a growing YA fantasy audience have shown that witchcraft, and all similarly categorised high school powers, have started to overtake the flagging superhero genre. But then why does something like Hexed still feel so dusty?

Like Wish, it’s a film clearly crafted by people who have deep affection for the Disney back catalogue but who can’t quite turn reverence for what came before into any real idea of where to take things going forward. Again, there’s something too calculated and businesslike, with nods to previous films and regurgitated life lessons, and while Disney adventures have always emerged from a Goliath-sized mega-corporation, the best ones can make you briefly forget that. Sure Disney might have, shamefully, tried to trademark Day of the Dead before the release of Coco (!) but the film itself was charming, sweet and genuinely moving. While the company might have turned Ratatouille into everything from a theme park ride to a branded set of cheese knives, thoughts of merchandise were not in one’s head while watching a rat’s thrilling journey from gourmand to head chef. But Hexed is too soulless and synthetically corporate to distract us from its ultimate Q4 marketing aims.

It takes place in a universe where witches have been Salem trialled away to another magic-filled realm (hello new Disney World section), where they live under the tyrannical control of Queen Celeste (voiced by Jodie Foster). A powerful young witch called Billie (Hailee Steinfeld) doesn’t yet know she’s a powerful young witch after her mother (Rashida Jones) decided to keep her talents hidden via a magic-suppressing bracelet (perfect merch op) forced on her wrist at a young age, a way to keep her safe in a world that does not take kindly to people like her. But as a rebellious teen, Billie discovers her true self and after a portal opens, she travels to the world of witches to team up with a three-eyed cat called Beef Roger Crummchuk (Walton Goggins, also a stuffed toy to be) to try to save her fellow witches from their evil queen.

It’s a story of mothers and daughters and how both can try to foster empathy for the other but even a lower-tier Disney film like Brave managed to teach this same lesson with far more skill and infinitely more heart. There’s no real joy or fizz in Billie’s discovery of her powers or ingenuity to how she then uses them and the film quickly starts to resemble not just a by-the-numbers, save-the-kingdom Disney tale but also a Marvel-like superhero adventure, especially in the numbingly effects-laden showdown finale. Foster has real command as a voice actor but her villain isn’t really villainous or distinctive enough, despite attempts to paint her as a recognisably authoritarian-like ruler. Goggins is a similarly effective vocal presence but, again, his sidekick isn’t written in a way that’s all that memorable with his dialogue, together with that of another anonymously underwritten owl sidekick, depressingly devoid of any spark or inventive humour. There’s also something a little cheap and inelegant about how he’s animated and coloured, similar to some purple-eyed henchwitches, who all look like they belong in a cheap Saturday morning cartoon not a big-budget Disney epic (the choice to score a giant action sequence with Demi Lovato’s Confident also feels notably unrefined). There’s an overly hectic style to too many scenes and a lack of grace to the set-pieces, more likely to induce a headache over a sense of awe, taking us further and further away from what used to elevate the studio far above its competitors.

There would be few greater big screen pleasures at this moment than a true return to form for Disney, an original, invigorating crowd-pleaser to rival what so many of us grew up watching and loving but Hexed is another hollow and glumly disappointing also-ran. Don’t tell Mickey but it’s perhaps telling that this month’s best new animated film about a rule-breaking goth girl dealing with spells and familial strife is actually on Netflix . Forget magic, the kingdom is in need of a miracle.

Hexed is out in US cinemas on 25 November, in Australian cinemas on 26 November and in the UK on 27 November

articles.title: World Chess Championship 2026 Game 1: Gukesh Dommaraju v Javokhir Sindarov – live
articles.summary: Youngest title match in chess history starts Tuesday Sindarov and Gukesh open Game 1 with Berlin defense Explainer: all your pre-match questions, answered Preview: Gukesh vows to win title ‘all over again’ Sindarov interview: ‘I can’t play games just for fun’ Play through 22 famous world championship games Bluesky Bryan at @BryanAGraham or email him The players have shaken hands and we’re off! We have a Berlin defense of the Ruy Lopez ( 1 e4 e5 2 Nf3 Nc6 3 Bb5 Nf6 ), one of the most thoroughly analyzed openings in modern chess. The Berlin famously helped Vladimir Kramnik dethrone Garry Kasparov in their 2000 world title match in London and has been a staple of elite chess ever since, earning a reputation as one of black’s most reliable weapons against 1 e4. Continue reading...
articles.content:
India’s Gukesh Dommaraju is defending the world chess championship against fast-rising Uzbek grandmaster Javokhir Sindarov in the youngest title match in the competition’s 140-year history. The best-of-14-games contest is scheduled to take place from 24 November to 12 December at the Fondation Martin Bodmer outside Geneva, with an overall prize fund of $2.5m (£1.9m).

Game 1 starts at 3pm in Geneva, 2pm in London, 9am in New York and 7.30pm in India

Sindarov will have the white pieces for Game 1 and make the first move

Gukesh and Sindarov are both 20 years old, making this the youngest matchup in world championship’s 140-year history

Read the Guardian’s comprehensive watch guide for the Gukesh v Sindarov showdown

Go move by move through 22 of the most famous games in world championship history

Gukesh marches his king further up the board ( 27 ... Kf6 ) rather than retreating. The champion is down to 8min 39sec for his next 13 moves, while Sindarov still has more than 25 minutes.

Things are heating up ( 25 ... Nc6 26 f5 gxf5 27 Nxf5+ ). Sindarov has recovered the pawn he lost and given check to Gukesh’s king.

And we have our first material imbalance of the game ( 23 ... Nxe5 24 f4 ). Gukesh has won a pawn but Sindarov has immediately attacked the knight that captured it. The champion responds by threatening Sindarov’s own knight on the kingside ( 24 ... g6 25 Ng3 ).

The challenger has retreated and now Gukesh must navigate a delicate position with barely 10 minutes to make his next 16 moves.

A flurry of activity on the board ( 22 Ne1 axb3 23 axb3 ). Gukesh has initiated an exchange of pawns on the queenside, opening up the a-file for his rook. The game is becoming more dynamic at a moment when the champion can least afford to spend time calculating variations.

Sindarov has been in the think tank for 15 minutes and counting , but his overwhelming time advantage affords him that luxury.

Meanwhile, over on the Chess.com broadcast, Judit Polgar is telling war stories. Sindarov’s decision to play 21 g4 rather than Stockfish’s preferred 21 Ne1 has reminded the Hungarian grandmaster of a painful defeat to Veselin Topalov in a similar Berlin endgame during the 2005 Fide world championship tournament in San Luis, Argentina.

“At some point I played g4,” Polgar recalls. “Not because I wanted to play for a win desperately, but because I thought that was the best move I could make in that position.

“And after the game people came to me: ‘Why did you play for a win in that position? It was not better anymore.’ I said: ‘I was not playing for a win in that position. I just thought that was the best move.’”

Two more moves ( 21 g4 Ke7 ) and Gukesh is putting his king to work in the center of the board. For all the Berlin’s reputation as a drawish opening, this is shaping up to be a three-result game.

Gukesh has pushed another pawn forward ( 19 ... c5 ), reinforcing his bishop on b4 and restricting the movement of white’s pieces. Sindarov quickly moves his knight to the edge of the board, prompting Gukesh to bring his rook across to defend his g7 pawn ( 20 Nh5 Rg8 ).

The champion has reached the halfway point to the first time control with barely 16 minutes to spare, while Sindarov still has more than 55 minutes at his disposal. The defending champion is effectively going to have to play rapid chess against an in-form opponent who has the luxury of thinking things through.

That said, despite Gukesh’s visible suffering, the Hungarian grandmaster Peter Leko is beginning to warm to black’s position on the official Fide broadcast.

“Nh5 was played clearly out of ambition,” Leko says. “I don’t know how much this choice was influenced by the clock situation, whether Sindarov wants to keep the game going because of the time situation. And I was praising the move Ng3 because of the clock factor. Looking at the position now, with the knight on h5 stuck and black having a clear b7-b5 push in the air, I already kind of wonder if I would not be much happier with black now.”

Gukesh has finally nudged his h-pawn forward ( 18 … h6 ), denying a square from Sindarov’s bishop and knights. Even if the position remains objectively equal, the clock is giving Sindarov a significant practical advantage.

Latvian grandmaster Arturs Neiksans has entered the chat , suggesting that Gukesh’s struggles today could have implications well beyond the opening game. Ra5), but one that would land the champion in trouble if Sindarov answered with 18 Bg5. An important decision awaits Gukesh, and he can ill afford to spend too much time making it.

Two more moves in Geneva ( 16 ... Be6 17 b3 ). Gukesh has moved his bishop out of the path of Sindarov’s rooks, while the challenger has reinforced his position on the queenside.

Given the decidedly bibliothecal setting, it’s a particularly fitting question. The Fondation Martin Bodmer is one of the world’s great repositories of rare books and manuscripts, its 160,000 treasures including a Gutenberg Bible, Shakespeare’s First Folio and a copy of Isaac Newton’s Principia Mathematica once owned by his great rival Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz.

“And yeah, a very exciting endgame ahead because there’s still a full board of pieces.”

Something for Sindarov, who has been mulling his response to 13 ... Bd7 for more than 20 minutes, to investigate when he finally gets his hands on the game after the world championship.

The American grandmaster Maurice Ashley has joined the official Fide broadcast and admits he was hoping for something a little more combustible than a Berlin endgame to get the match under way.

“Obviously, the Berlin is one of those you see and you go, ‘Oh, OK, how’s he going to break down this wall?’ It’s obviously a big challenge when you have the white pieces, but clearly it looked like Sindarov was well prepared for this eventuality. So I’m excited to see the match get off, but it would have been nice to see something wild, crazy, queens on the board.

“I feel like [Hungarian grandmaster] Peter Leko here is excited by these kinds of positions. We were talking about endgames and his ability when he was young to play these extremely well. But I think the fans probably wanted some more sauce.”

And finally Gukesh makes his move! After a think of more than 15 minutes, the world champion has opted for 13 ... Bd7 , bringing his last minor piece into play. The bishop also shields the black king from a potential check along the d-file, giving Gukesh greater flexibility in repositioning his king and coordinating his rooks. He’s more than 35 minutes behind the challenger on time, though.

Gukesh is in another deep think as Javokhir leaves the board for the nearby lounge chair inside the cramped playing hall.

Gukesh has developed his dark-squared bishop and Sindarov has centralized his queenside knight ( 12 ... Be7 13 Ne4 ). The pace of play has slowed considerably as the players begin to grapple with the strategic subtleties of the Berlin. Both Stockfish and the Sesse supercomputer assess the position as dead even (0.00).

An email from the always welcome Gary Naylor , who sees parallels between the world chess championship and another of Europe’s great endurance events:

Given the location, the schedule, the fact that each leader has a team supporting him and, more than anything, the stamina required, this feels like the Tour de France. I suppose players have the ability to make stages – games – hard or easy by their strategies too.

No lycra to report, Gary, but there’s certainly something to the analogy. The ability to conserve energy over a three-week campaign, knowing when to attack and when to settle for a quiet day, is an underrated component of world championship matchplay.

Gukesh has been mulling his response to 12 Be3 for more than 10 minutes , after spending about eight minutes on his previous move.

“He still knows the position, but he is taking time to make sure he makes the right moves,” Russian grandmaster Peter Svidler says on the official Fide broadcast. “But Gukesh is already down almost 18 minutes on the clock. Considering he’s playing one of the most topical openings of the past 25 years, that’s some time expenditure.”

We’re heading straight into the famous Berlin endgame ( 4 O-O Nxe4 5 d4 Nd6 6 Bxc6 dxc6 7 dxe5 Nf5 8 Qxd8+ Kxd8 ). The Berlin famously helped Vladimir Kramnik dethrone Garry Kasparov in their 2000 world title match in London and has been a staple of elite chess ever since, earning a reputation as one of black’s most reliable weapons against 1 e4.

We’re eight minutes to the scheduled first move , but American grandmaster Maurice Ashley has started with his introduction of the players to the playing hall. Gukesh enters first and takes his seat behind the black pieces. Sindarov, playing as white after Sunday’s drawing of lots, enters second.

If you’re looking for some pre-match reading, the Guardian spoke exclusively with Javokhir Sindarov on Sunday about his meteoric rise, his love of Lionel Messi, his plans to play GTA VI once the match is over and why chess’s happy warrior believes there’s more to life than the game. A taste:

“I’m the guy who can’t play games just for fun,” Sindarov tells the Guardian less than 48 hours before Tuesday’s world championship opener in Geneva, smiling at the absurdity of it. “If I play something, I always try to learn, trying to become better.”

That means poring over Counter-Strike tactics and watching YouTube tutorials before joining in with his mates. There is, it appears, no such thing as a casual game in Sindarov’s world, much less a friendly. “I always like to beat my friends,” he says. “I watch some video lessons and then come and beat them after some tournaments. I think the best thing is to beat your friends in some game.”

It is a revealing admission from a young man who has acquired a reputation for being uncommonly relaxed at the chess board. While many of the world’s elite players seem to carry the weight of every position on their shoulders – the viral clip of Sergey Karjakin agonizing for 25 minutes over a move during the 2016 world title match remains a cult classic in chess circles – Sindarov frequently gives off the impression of someone who is simply enjoying himself. The easygoing mien of the sport’s happy warrior is a quality that has caught his opponent’s attention. “One thing I learned from Sindarov is that he seems to be so happy while playing chess,” Gukesh Dommaraju, the reigning world champion, said in an interview published last week.

We’ve gone through the 140-year history of the world championship and chosen 22 of the most memorable games. You can go move by move through each of them here . It’s the perfect timesuck in the final run-up to today’s first move.

From the middle of the 16th century, there have come down to us the names of chess players who have been widely regarded as the strongest of their time. The earliest of these was the Spanish priest Ruy López de Segura, after whom one of the most popular openings of modern times is named. Others who followed include the Calabrese Gioachino Greco , François-André Danican Philidor , Louis-Charles Mahé de La Bourdonnais , Alexander McDonnell , Howard Staunton , Adolf Anderssen , Mikhail Chigorin and Paul Morphy , each of whom are lionized for their contributions to the development of theory and strategy as well as their dominance over their board during their respective eras.

But not until Wilhelm Steinitz and Johannes Zukertort sat down in a small room at 80 Fifth Avenue in New York City on the afternoon of 11 January 1886 did a formal competition to determine the best player on the planet come to pass. Their first-to-10-wins encounter was held in three US cities over the next 78 days for a prize fund of $4,000. Since then, the world chess championship has provided the stage for countless unforgettable contests showcasing the precision, imagination and brilliance of the royal game at the highest level.

The legitimacy of the world championship, of course, remains a subject of lively debate. The absence of Magnus Carlsen continues to cast a long shadow over the sport’s showcase event. The 35-year-old Norwegian has held the world No 1 ranking for more than 15 consecutive years and was widely regarded as the game’s strongest player even before he defeated Vishy Anand for the world title in 2013. He only strengthened his claim as the greatest player of any era in 2021, when he crushed Ian Nepomniachtchi in Dubai in his fourth successful defense of the crown.

But Carlsen declined to defend his title for a fifth time in 2023, citing a lack of motivation to endure the months-long grind of preparation that championship matches demand. Only twice before had the chain of succession that stretches back to Wilhelm Steinitz in 1886 been broken: when Alexander Alekhine died as champion in 1946 and when Bobby Fischer forfeited the title in 1975.

Ding Liren went on to defeat Nepomniachtchi for the vacant title before losing it to Gukesh Dommaraju in Singapore the following year. Now Gukesh faces Sindarov in a match between two 20-year-olds ranked No 26 and No 4 in the world respectively, while the planet’s top-ranked player remains on the sidelines – at a time when his No 1 ranking is looking more vulnerable than any time in anyone’s memory. The generational stakes are undeniable, but the question that has dogged the championship since Carlsen walked away remains unresolved: can the winner truly claim to be the best chess player in the world?

For two elite players born in the same general part of the world barely six months apart, their competitive history is remarkably sparse: just three encounters in classical chess. Sindarov holds a 2½-½ advantage with two wins and one draw in their lifetime head-to-head, which dates back to their first encounter as tweens at the Moscow Open in 2018. Their most recent meeting happened in January at the prestigious Tata Steel tournament in Wijk aan Zee, where a tense positional struggle gave way to a wild, time-scrambled endgame before the pair settled for a draw after 78 moves. Sindarov also holds a 2-1 edge in their three rapid and blitz contests this year.

Gukesh’s form has largely gone off the rails since reaching the summit 23 months ago in Singapore. After making it to No 3 in the world with a peak rating of 2794, the Indian suffered a prolonged run of disappointing results, including a joint-last finish at March’s Prague Chess Festival and last-place showings at Norway Chess and the Chennai Grand Masters. He subsequently withdrew from the classical portion of the Grand Chess Tour and had tumbled to No 32 in the rankings by September, when his live rating briefly dipped below the 2700 barrier for the first time in four years, although his performances improved at that month’s Chess Olympiad.

Many of the world’s top grandmasters have expressed deep pessimism about Gukesh’s chances in Geneva due to his lengthy slump and Sindarov’s sustained upward tick. So too have the bookmakers, who have installed the Uzbek as a clear frontrunner at roughly 1-3 odds despite Gukesh being the champion. Carlsen has described Sindarov as “a pretty significant favorite”, citing the Indian’s tendency to take excessive risks. “His evaluations are way too optimistic,” the world No 1 said recently . “That makes him take way more chances than he should. I think especially now his confidence hasn’t been too high, he just tries to do a little bit too much.”

Yet one factor in Gukesh’s favor is his firsthand experience in the cauldron of a world championship match, where the intense psychological and physical rigors of facing the same opponent for weeks on end can be as punishing as the chess itself. Caruana, the world No 3 and former world title challenger who pushed Carlsen to the brink in 2018, has cautioned against writing off the champion despite his struggles. “The kind of ability he had – or has, whatever you want to say – it doesn’t disappear overnight,” Caruana said in September . “So, in my opinion, it can reverse at any moment.”

Here’s a review of the format for the world championship match . Gukesh and Sindarov will play up to 14 classical games with each player awarded one point for a win and a half-point for a draw. Whoever reaches seven and a half points first will be declared the champion (and no dead rubbers will be played).

The time control for each game is 120 minutes per side for the first 40 moves, then 30 minutes for the remainder of the game, with a 30-second increment per move starting with move 41. That means games can stretch beyond seven hours , testing both players’ concentration and endurance. Players are not permitted to agree to a draw before black’s 40th move, a rule designed to discourage short, uneventful games. A draw claim before then is only allowed in the case of threefold repetition or stalemate, subject to approval by the chief arbiter or deputy arbiter.

If the score is level after 14 games, a series of tiebreaks will be played on 12 December, starting with four rapid games at 15 minutes per player plus 10 seconds per move. If still tied, the players will contest two games at 10 minutes plus five seconds, followed if necessary by two blitz games at three minutes plus two seconds. Further single blitz games will be played until a winner emerges. Three of the past five world championship matches have been deadlocked after the classical portion and required tiebreaks: 2016 , 2018 and 2023 .

Hello and welcome to Geneva for day one of the World Chess Championship. Over the next three weeks, India’s defending champion Gukesh Dommaraju and Javokhir Sindarov of Uzbekistan will compete in a scheduled best-of-14-games match for the sport’s most prestigious title and a share of a $2.5m prize fund. The setting is the Fondation Martin Bodmer in Cologny, an affluent suburb overlooking Lake Geneva, where the two 20-year-olds will make history as the youngest pairing ever to contest a world championship match in the competition’s 140-year history.

Gukesh became the youngest undisputed world chess champion in history when he defeated China’s Ding Liren in Singapore in December 2024, aged just 18, shattering the record held by Garry Kasparov, who was 22 when he dethroned Anatoly Karpov in 1985. An aggressive player known for creating sharp, tactically complex positions aimed at unsettling opponents, the Chennai-born grandmaster has struggled badly for form since winning the crown, sliding from a career-high No 3 to No 26 in the world rankings and raising questions over his chances of retaining the title in his first defense.

Sindarov, meanwhile, has emerged as one of the most formidable talents of a new generation of Uzbek grandmasters. Born in Tashkent, he became a grandmaster at 12 years and 10 months, the second-youngest in history at the time, and secured his place in Geneva by winning the eight-man Candidates tournament earlier this year. A fearless, resourceful player in a rich vein of form, he enters his first world championship match ranked fourth in the world, up from No 25 last year and a remarkable 22 places above the reigning champion, and with a favorable head-to-head record against Gukesh in classical chess.

We’re roughly 80 minutes away from the ceremonial opening moves. Fide president Timur Turlov will do the honors for white, with five-time world champion and Fide deputy president Viswanathan Anand moving for black. Plenty more to come between now and then.

The American grandmaster Maurice Ashley has joined the official Fide broadcast and admits he was hoping for something a little more combustible than a Berlin endgame to get the match under way.

“Obviously, the Berlin is one of those you see and you go, ‘Oh, OK, how’s he going to break down this wall?’ It’s obviously a big challenge when you have the white pieces, but clearly it looked like Sindarov was well prepared for this eventuality. So I’m excited to see the match get off, but it would have been nice to see something wild, crazy, queens on the board.

“I feel like [Hungarian grandmaster] Peter Leko here is excited by these kinds of positions. We were talking about endgames and his ability when he was young to play these extremely well. But I think the fans probably wanted some more sauce.”

And finally Gukesh makes his move! After a think of more than 15 minutes, the world champion has opted for 13 ... Bd7 , bringing his last minor piece into play. The bishop also shields the black king from a potential check along the d-file, giving Gukesh greater flexibility in repositioning his king and coordinating his rooks. He’s more than 35 minutes behind the challenger on time, though.
Gukesh is in another deep think as Javokhir leaves the board for the nearby lounge chair inside the cramped playing hall.

“Now I understand what Javokhir was playing for,” English grandmaster David Howell says on the Chess .com broadcast. “I would have expected this opening from two older players, not maybe two 20-year-olds. But now I understand he’s trying to bait Gukesh. He’s trying to tempt him into some line where he has a deep, deep idea. Yeah, it’s very provocative.”

Gukesh has developed his dark-squared bishop and Sindarov has centralized his queenside knight ( 12 ... Be7 13 Ne4 ). The pace of play has slowed considerably as the players begin to grapple with the strategic subtleties of the Berlin. Both Stockfish and the Sesse supercomputer assess the position as dead even (0.00).
An email from the always welcome Gary Naylor , who sees parallels between the world chess championship and another of Europe’s great endurance events:

Given the location, the schedule, the fact that each leader has a team supporting him and, more than anything, the stamina required, this feels like the Tour de France. I suppose players have the ability to make stages – games – hard or easy by their strategies too.

No lycra to report, Gary, but there’s certainly something to the analogy. The ability to conserve energy over a three-week campaign, knowing when to attack and when to settle for a quiet day, is an underrated component of world championship matchplay.
Gukesh has been mulling his response to 12 Be3 for more than 10 minutes , after spending about eight minutes on his previous move.

“He still knows the position, but he is taking time to make sure he makes the right moves,” Russian grandmaster Peter Svidler says on the official Fide broadcast. “But Gukesh is already down almost 18 minutes on the clock. Considering he’s playing one of the most topical openings of the past 25 years, that’s some time expenditure.”
Gukesh has brought his knight to g6, putting pressure on the advanced white pawn on e5, and Sindarov has continued his development by bringing his bishop into play ( 11 ... Ng6 12 Be3 ).

Gukesh has returned his king to its original square and rerouted his knight ( 9 Rd1+ Ke8 10 Nc3 Ne7 11 h3 ). Sindarov’s last move prevents black’s light-squared bishop from coming to g4 and pinning the knight on f3, while giving his own king some breathing room.

“I think it’s important to highlight for our viewers that black is not playing for a draw,” the Hungarian grandmaster Judit Polgár says on Chess .com’s broadcast. “Black is just deciding to go into an endgame or a middlegame without queens, where it seems like only white has a slight edge. Black has doubled pawns on c6 and c7, black has the bishop pair, but basically black can go b6, develop the pieces properly.”

We’re heading straight into the famous Berlin endgame ( 4 O-O Nxe4 5 d4 Nd6 6 Bxc6 dxc6 7 dxe5 Nf5 8 Qxd8+ Kxd8 ). The queens are off the board after only eight moves, leaving white with a kingside pawn majority and black with the bishop pair but doubled c-pawns and a king that has forfeited the right to castle.

Don’t mistake the early exchange of queens for a lack of ambition. The resulting position is deceptively rich in strategic possibilities and has been the subject of decades of analysis at the highest level. Gukesh has continued with 9 Rd1+ , and both players are still moving quickly.
The players have shaken hands and we’re off! We have a Berlin defense of the Ruy Lopez ( 1 e4 e5 2 Nf3 Nc6 3 Bb5 Nf6 ), one of the most thoroughly analyzed openings in modern chess.

The Berlin famously helped Vladimir Kramnik dethrone Garry Kasparov in their 2000 world title match in London and has been a staple of elite chess ever since, earning a reputation as one of black’s most reliable weapons against 1 e4.

We’re eight minutes to the scheduled first move , but American grandmaster Maurice Ashley has started with his introduction of the players to the playing hall. Gukesh enters first and takes his seat behind the black pieces. Sindarov, playing as white after Sunday’s drawing of lots, enters second.

If you’re looking for some pre-match reading, the Guardian spoke exclusively with Javokhir Sindarov on Sunday about his meteoric rise, his love of Lionel Messi, his plans to play GTA VI once the match is over and why chess’s happy warrior believes there’s more to life than the game. A taste:

“I’m the guy who can’t play games just for fun,” Sindarov tells the Guardian less than 48 hours before Tuesday’s world championship opener in Geneva, smiling at the absurdity of it. “If I play something, I always try to learn, trying to become better.”

That means poring over Counter-Strike tactics and watching YouTube tutorials before joining in with his mates. There is, it appears, no such thing as a casual game in Sindarov’s world, much less a friendly. “I always like to beat my friends,” he says. “I watch some video lessons and then come and beat them after some tournaments. I think the best thing is to beat your friends in some game.”

It is a revealing admission from a young man who has acquired a reputation for being uncommonly relaxed at the chess board. While many of the world’s elite players seem to carry the weight of every position on their shoulders – the viral clip of Sergey Karjakin agonizing for 25 minutes over a move during the 2016 world title match remains a cult classic in chess circles – Sindarov frequently gives off the impression of someone who is simply enjoying himself. The easygoing mien of the sport’s happy warrior is a quality that has caught his opponent’s attention. “One thing I learned from Sindarov is that he seems to be so happy while playing chess,” Gukesh Dommaraju, the reigning world champion, said in an interview published last week.

We’ve gone through the 140-year history of the world championship and chosen 22 of the most memorable games. You can go move by move through each of them here . It’s the perfect timesuck in the final run-up to today’s first move.

From the middle of the 16th century, there have come down to us the names of chess players who have been widely regarded as the strongest of their time. The earliest of these was the Spanish priest Ruy López de Segura, after whom one of the most popular openings of modern times is named. Others who followed include the Calabrese Gioachino Greco , François-André Danican Philidor , Louis-Charles Mahé de La Bourdonnais , Alexander McDonnell , Howard Staunton , Adolf Anderssen , Mikhail Chigorin and Paul Morphy , each of whom are lionized for their contributions to the development of theory and strategy as well as their dominance over their board during their respective eras.

But not until Wilhelm Steinitz and Johannes Zukertort sat down in a small room at 80 Fifth Avenue in New York City on the afternoon of 11 January 1886 did a formal competition to determine the best player on the planet come to pass. Their first-to-10-wins encounter was held in three US cities over the next 78 days for a prize fund of $4,000. Since then, the world chess championship has provided the stage for countless unforgettable contests showcasing the precision, imagination and brilliance of the royal game at the highest level.

The legitimacy of the world championship, of course, remains a subject of lively debate. The absence of Magnus Carlsen continues to cast a long shadow over the sport’s showcase event. The 35-year-old Norwegian has held the world No 1 ranking for more than 15 consecutive years and was widely regarded as the game’s strongest player even before he defeated Vishy Anand for the world title in 2013. He only strengthened his claim as the greatest player of any era in 2021, when he crushed Ian Nepomniachtchi in Dubai in his fourth successful defense of the crown.

But Carlsen declined to defend his title for a fifth time in 2023, citing a lack of motivation to endure the months-long grind of preparation that championship matches demand. Only twice before had the chain of succession that stretches back to Wilhelm Steinitz in 1886 been broken: when Alexander Alekhine died as champion in 1946 and when Bobby Fischer forfeited the title in 1975.

Ding Liren went on to defeat Nepomniachtchi for the vacant title before losing it to Gukesh Dommaraju in Singapore the following year. Now Gukesh faces Sindarov in a match between two 20-year-olds ranked No 26 and No 4 in the world respectively, while the planet’s top-ranked player remains on the sidelines – at a time when his No 1 ranking is looking more vulnerable than any time in anyone’s memory. The generational stakes are undeniable, but the question that has dogged the championship since Carlsen walked away remains unresolved: can the winner truly claim to be the best chess player in the world?

For two elite players born in the same general part of the world barely six months apart, their competitive history is remarkably sparse: just three encounters in classical chess. Sindarov holds a 2½-½ advantage with two wins and one draw in their lifetime head-to-head, which dates back to their first encounter as tweens at the Moscow Open in 2018. Their most recent meeting happened in January at the prestigious Tata Steel tournament in Wijk aan Zee, where a tense positional struggle gave way to a wild, time-scrambled endgame before the pair settled for a draw after 78 moves. Sindarov also holds a 2-1 edge in their three rapid and blitz contests this year.

Gukesh’s form has largely gone off the rails since reaching the summit 23 months ago in Singapore. After making it to No 3 in the world with a peak rating of 2794, the Indian suffered a prolonged run of disappointing results, including a joint-last finish at March’s Prague Chess Festival and last-place showings at Norway Chess and the Chennai Grand Masters. He subsequently withdrew from the classical portion of the Grand Chess Tour and had tumbled to No 32 in the rankings by September, when his live rating briefly dipped below the 2700 barrier for the first time in four years, although his performances improved at that month’s Chess Olympiad.

Many of the world’s top grandmasters have expressed deep pessimism about Gukesh’s chances in Geneva due to his lengthy slump and Sindarov’s sustained upward tick. So too have the bookmakers, who have installed the Uzbek as a clear frontrunner at roughly 1-3 odds despite Gukesh being the champion. Carlsen has described Sindarov as “a pretty significant favorite”, citing the Indian’s tendency to take excessive risks. “His evaluations are way too optimistic,” the world No 1 said recently . “That makes him take way more chances than he should. I think especially now his confidence hasn’t been too high, he just tries to do a little bit too much.”

Yet one factor in Gukesh’s favor is his firsthand experience in the cauldron of a world championship match, where the intense psychological and physical rigors of facing the same opponent for weeks on end can be as punishing as the chess itself. Caruana, the world No 3 and former world title challenger who pushed Carlsen to the brink in 2018, has cautioned against writing off the champion despite his struggles. “The kind of ability he had – or has, whatever you want to say – it doesn’t disappear overnight,” Caruana said in September . “So, in my opinion, it can reverse at any moment.”

Here’s a review of the format for the world championship match . Gukesh and Sindarov will play up to 14 classical games with each player awarded one point for a win and a half-point for a draw. Whoever reaches seven and a half points first will be declared the champion (and no dead rubbers will be played).

The time control for each game is 120 minutes per side for the first 40 moves, then 30 minutes for the remainder of the game, with a 30-second increment per move starting with move 41. That means games can stretch beyond seven hours , testing both players’ concentration and endurance. Players are not permitted to agree to a draw before black’s 40th move, a rule designed to discourage short, uneventful games. A draw claim before then is only allowed in the case of threefold repetition or stalemate, subject to approval by the chief arbiter or deputy arbiter.

If the score is level after 14 games, a series of tiebreaks will be played on 12 December, starting with four rapid games at 15 minutes per player plus 10 seconds per move. If still tied, the players will contest two games at 10 minutes plus five seconds, followed if necessary by two blitz games at three minutes plus two seconds. Further single blitz games will be played until a winner emerges. Three of the past five world championship matches have been deadlocked after the classical portion and required tiebreaks: 2016 , 2018 and 2023 .

Hello and welcome to Geneva for day one of the World Chess Championship. Over the next three weeks, India’s defending champion Gukesh Dommaraju and Javokhir Sindarov of Uzbekistan will compete in a scheduled best-of-14-games match for the sport’s most prestigious title and a share of a $2.5m prize fund. The setting is the Fondation Martin Bodmer in Cologny, an affluent suburb overlooking Lake Geneva, where the two 20-year-olds will make history as the youngest pairing ever to contest a world championship match in the competition’s 140-year history.

Gukesh became the youngest undisputed world chess champion in history when he defeated China’s Ding Liren in Singapore in December 2024, aged just 18, shattering the record held by Garry Kasparov, who was 22 when he dethroned Anatoly Karpov in 1985. An aggressive player known for creating sharp, tactically complex positions aimed at unsettling opponents, the Chennai-born grandmaster has struggled badly for form since winning the crown, sliding from a career-high No 3 to No 26 in the world rankings and raising questions over his chances of retaining the title in his first defense.

Sindarov, meanwhile, has emerged as one of the most formidable talents of a new generation of Uzbek grandmasters. Born in Tashkent, he became a grandmaster at 12 years and 10 months, the second-youngest in history at the time, and secured his place in Geneva by winning the eight-man Candidates tournament earlier this year. A fearless, resourceful player in a rich vein of form, he enters his first world championship match ranked fourth in the world, up from No 25 last year and a remarkable 22 places above the reigning champion, and with a favorable head-to-head record against Gukesh in classical chess.

We’re roughly 80 minutes away from the ceremonial opening moves. Fide president Timur Turlov will do the honors for white, with five-time world champion and Fide deputy president Viswanathan Anand moving for black. Plenty more to come between now and then.
Bryan will be here shortly. In the meantime here’s our watch guide for this year’s World Chess Championship,
