articles.title: Turkey gets a glowup: how a Chinese BBQ spot remade the Thanksgiving bird
articles.summary: Chicago’s Sun Wah BBQ started a new Turkey Day tradition for immigrants and other neighbors: allowing them to bring in their fowl and roast it in the fragrant Hong Kong-style Tell us: do you have a special new year food tradition? Behind an Uptown Chicago facade of glass and green-glazed bricks, rows of mahogany-red ducks glisten. This neighborhood is sometimes called “New Chinatown”, sometimes “Little Vietnam ”. And this tidy restaurant is Sun Wah BBQ , which Eric and Lynda Cheng opened in 1987. Today, it’s also an unlikely Thanksgiving destination. Continue reading...
articles.content:
Chicago’s Sun Wah BBQ started a new Turkey Day tradition for immigrants and other neighbors: allowing them to bring in their fowl and roast it in the fragrant Hong Kong-style

Behind an Uptown Chicago facade of glass and green-glazed bricks, rows of mahogany-red ducks glisten.

This neighborhood is sometimes called “New Chinatown”, sometimes “Little Vietnam ”. And this tidy restaurant is Sun Wah BBQ , which Eric and Lynda Cheng opened in 1987. Today, it’s also an unlikely Thanksgiving destination.

Every November, customers bring their own turkeys to Sun Wah to be prepared in the style of a Hong Kong roast duck. This year, the Cheng family will roast close to 200 turkeys, thanks to a TikTok video that increased demand. But this annual tradition, turning pale workaday turkeys into gorgeously lacquered holiday centerpieces, began as an informal favor about two decades ago.

The first requests came from immigrant families in the neighborhood, recalled co-owner and manager Kelly Cheng, Eric and Lynda’s daughter. Eric had fled mainland China for Hong Kong in the 1970s, married Lynda, and apprenticed in Chinese barbecue, where meats are roasted in extremely hot ovens rather than smoked low and slow, like most American barbecue. The couple eventually settled in New York City, where Eric worked in Chinatown restaurants and opened his own. Then, on a visit to Chicago, the Chengs saw a gap: what they call the “food of emperors” was underrepresented in the city.

Another gap became apparent after the Chengs opened shop in the Windy City, this time between immigrant workers and their employers. Chinese, Vietnamese and Thai residents were often flummoxed by a holiday gift from their workplaces: turkeys for Thanksgiving and hams for Christmas. For many, the turkey was an unfamiliar bird – not to mention the full Thanksgiving spread.

“It came frozen, so they just stuck it back in the freezer,” said Kelly. “Come spring, they’re cleaning out their freezer and a lot of them shop at our restaurant, so they came in and were like, ‘Can you cook this?’ That’s how it started.”

At first, Sun Wah tried standard “American-style” oven-roasting and spatchcocking. The results were decidedly mixed: undercooked, overcooked, bland or oversalted. The family was upfront about their own inexperience: “We don’t know how, well, we’ll do it, but we’ll do it for you.”

Over time, the Chengs adapted Eric’s Chinese barbecue techniques for a much larger, less forgiving bird. “We’ll cook it Chinese-style, where it’s going to be a flavor we like,” said Kelly.

Roasted duck is a centuries-old culinary tradition in China. The Chengs specifically prepare their turkey in the Hong Kong- or Cantonese- style , where the bird is stuffed with aromatics, different from the peking duck method , where air is pushed under the fowl’s skin and the meat is expertly carved into thin slices. The Chengs treat the turkey’s cavity with bean paste, five-spice blend, cilantro, shallots and ginger, working a mixture of dry and wet seasonings into each bird before letting it air-dry for a day.

The turkeys then roast, hanging, inside the restaurant’s custom-built vertical vaults at 500F for two to four hours. The fat renders. The skin crisps. The meat stays succulently moist.

For years, Sun Wah’s turkey service managed to be both a neighborhood tradition and something of a local secret. TikTok, however, changed that.

Typically, the Chengs quietly begin taking orders online and by phone in early November, charging $8 per pound for a restaurant-supplied turkey customers will pick up around Thanksgiving or $5.50 per pound for customers who bring their own. This year, someone beat them to it.

The video came from Kate Bachman, a Chicago-based creator who shares apartment cooking, creative hosting ideas and neighborhood food discoveries. Bachman first tried Sun Wah’s turkey at a Friendsgiving two years earlier, hosted by a friend who dubbed the occasion “ThanksPeking”. The bird was so delicious she was still thinking about it two years later, when she hosted her own gathering and brought a turkey to Sun Wah herself.

“Especially when hosting in a small kitchen like I do, outsourcing the turkey makes timing the oven schedule way more manageable,” she said. She wanted to share the discovery with others who might appreciate a less stressful Thanksgiving.

But for Sun Wah, the unexpected publicity was a mixed blessing. The restaurant was flooded with calls from first-time customers. Longtime customers who had been bringing in their birds for 10 years were calling, hoping the Chengs could squeeze them in.

Kelly didn’t grow up dreaming of running a restaurant. She jokes that she learned to manage one before finishing grade school, but after graduating college she wanted some distance from the family business. She thought she found it in Hong Kong.

“Only to find that halfway across the world, I’m sitting in my rented condo watching bootleg videos and thinking, ‘I am freaking bored,’” she said on a recent Friday afternoon in the Sun Wah dining room before dinner service. “I realized I missed the noise.”

Thanksgiving at the restaurant certainly provides it. For the Chengs, the holiday begins days early. On Thanksgiving morning, Kelly’s brother Michael has the ovens running by 4.30am; Kelly arrives a few hours later, and by 8:30, the restaurant’s dozen or so employees are working at full steam.

The Thanksgiving roasting bonanza is a logistical juggling act that has prompted some disagreement within the family. Her semi-retired father, Eric, is enthusiastic about taking more orders. Kelly’s siblings, Michael and Laura, who still work in the kitchen as the barbecue chef and executive chef, are less convinced.

The restaurant remains open for dine-in and carry-out service. The roasting chambers turn out Chinese barbecue while the front kitchen keeps up with orders for noodles, congee and dim sum. Turkey customers may also order beef chow fun, Yang Chow fried rice, baby bok choy or potstickers.

Soon, they’ll file through the anise- and cinnamon-perfumed lobby, collecting their barbecued birds and heading home to bustling Thanksgiving tables. And what began as a practical solution for immigrant neighbors has become something larger: a Thanksgiving tradition embraced by longtime regulars and newcomers alike. In a city like Chicago, shaped by generations of immigration, Sun Wah’s turkeys are a reminder that American holiday traditions aren’t simply inherited. They’re adapted, reinvented and passed from one table to another.

The Chengs’ own holiday dinner comes later, perhaps over hot pot after the restaurant closes. Often, it came the following Sunday, when the family gathered at her grandmother’s house.

There, Kelly’s grandmother made congee from the leftover roasted bird. The bones gave the rice porridge a deeply savory flavor, and she added soft, boiled peanuts because Kelly’s grandfather loved them.

“It wasn’t my favorite kind of congee,” Kelly recalled. But it was the flavor that mattered. “You can’t top roasted turkey congee.”

The Guardian’s Feast app brings flavors from around the globe to your table, with more than 7,000 recipes spanning dozens of cuisines, each curated by food experts who truly know them.
paragraphs: Chicago’s Sun Wah BBQ started a new Turkey Day tradition for immigrants and other neighbors: allowing them to bring in their fowl and roast it in the fragrant Hong Kong-style
Behind an Uptown Chicago facade of glass and green-glazed bricks, rows of mahogany-red ducks glisten.

This neighborhood is sometimes called “New Chinatown”, sometimes “Little Vietnam ”. And this tidy restaurant is Sun Wah BBQ , which Eric and Lynda Cheng opened in 1987. Today, it’s also an unlikely Thanksgiving destination.

Every November, customers bring their own turkeys to Sun Wah to be prepared in the style of a Hong Kong roast duck. This year, the Cheng family will roast close to 200 turkeys, thanks to a TikTok video that increased demand. But this annual tradition, turning pale workaday turkeys into gorgeously lacquered holiday centerpieces, began as an informal favor about two decades ago.

The first requests came from immigrant families in the neighborhood, recalled co-owner and manager Kelly Cheng, Eric and Lynda’s daughter. Eric had fled mainland China for Hong Kong in the 1970s, married Lynda, and apprenticed in Chinese barbecue, where meats are roasted in extremely hot ovens rather than smoked low and slow, like most American barbecue. The couple eventually settled in New York City, where Eric worked in Chinatown restaurants and opened his own. Then, on a visit to Chicago, the Chengs saw a gap: what they call the “food of emperors” was underrepresented in the city.

Another gap became apparent after the Chengs opened shop in the Windy City, this time between immigrant workers and their employers. Chinese, Vietnamese and Thai residents were often flummoxed by a holiday gift from their workplaces: turkeys for Thanksgiving and hams for Christmas. For many, the turkey was an unfamiliar bird – not to mention the full Thanksgiving spread.

“It came frozen, so they just stuck it back in the freezer,” said Kelly. “Come spring, they’re cleaning out their freezer and a lot of them shop at our restaurant, so they came in and were like, ‘Can you cook this?’ That’s how it started.”

At first, Sun Wah tried standard “American-style” oven-roasting and spatchcocking. The results were decidedly mixed: undercooked, overcooked, bland or oversalted. The family was upfront about their own inexperience: “We don’t know how, well, we’ll do it, but we’ll do it for you.”
Over time, the Chengs adapted Eric’s Chinese barbecue techniques for a much larger, less forgiving bird. “We’ll cook it Chinese-style, where it’s going to be a flavor we like,” said Kelly.

Roasted duck is a centuries-old culinary tradition in China. The Chengs specifically prepare their turkey in the Hong Kong- or Cantonese- style , where the bird is stuffed with aromatics, different from the peking duck method , where air is pushed under the fowl’s skin and the meat is expertly carved into thin slices. The Chengs treat the turkey’s cavity with bean paste, five-spice blend, cilantro, shallots and ginger, working a mixture of dry and wet seasonings into each bird before letting it air-dry for a day.
The turkeys then roast, hanging, inside the restaurant’s custom-built vertical vaults at 500F for two to four hours. The fat renders. The skin crisps. The meat stays succulently moist.
For years, Sun Wah’s turkey service managed to be both a neighborhood tradition and something of a local secret. TikTok, however, changed that.

Typically, the Chengs quietly begin taking orders online and by phone in early November, charging $8 per pound for a restaurant-supplied turkey customers will pick up around Thanksgiving or $5.50 per pound for customers who bring their own. This year, someone beat them to it.

The video came from Kate Bachman, a Chicago-based creator who shares apartment cooking, creative hosting ideas and neighborhood food discoveries. Bachman first tried Sun Wah’s turkey at a Friendsgiving two years earlier, hosted by a friend who dubbed the occasion “ThanksPeking”. The bird was so delicious she was still thinking about it two years later, when she hosted her own gathering and brought a turkey to Sun Wah herself.

“Especially when hosting in a small kitchen like I do, outsourcing the turkey makes timing the oven schedule way more manageable,” she said. She wanted to share the discovery with others who might appreciate a less stressful Thanksgiving.

But for Sun Wah, the unexpected publicity was a mixed blessing. The restaurant was flooded with calls from first-time customers. Longtime customers who had been bringing in their birds for 10 years were calling, hoping the Chengs could squeeze them in.

Kelly didn’t grow up dreaming of running a restaurant. She jokes that she learned to manage one before finishing grade school, but after graduating college she wanted some distance from the family business. She thought she found it in Hong Kong.

“Only to find that halfway across the world, I’m sitting in my rented condo watching bootleg videos and thinking, ‘I am freaking bored,’” she said on a recent Friday afternoon in the Sun Wah dining room before dinner service. “I realized I missed the noise.”

Thanksgiving at the restaurant certainly provides it. For the Chengs, the holiday begins days early. On Thanksgiving morning, Kelly’s brother Michael has the ovens running by 4.30am; Kelly arrives a few hours later, and by 8:30, the restaurant’s dozen or so employees are working at full steam.

The Thanksgiving roasting bonanza is a logistical juggling act that has prompted some disagreement within the family. Her semi-retired father, Eric, is enthusiastic about taking more orders. Kelly’s siblings, Michael and Laura, who still work in the kitchen as the barbecue chef and executive chef, are less convinced.

The restaurant remains open for dine-in and carry-out service. The roasting chambers turn out Chinese barbecue while the front kitchen keeps up with orders for noodles, congee and dim sum. Turkey customers may also order beef chow fun, Yang Chow fried rice, baby bok choy or potstickers.

Soon, they’ll file through the anise- and cinnamon-perfumed lobby, collecting their barbecued birds and heading home to bustling Thanksgiving tables. And what began as a practical solution for immigrant neighbors has become something larger: a Thanksgiving tradition embraced by longtime regulars and newcomers alike. In a city like Chicago, shaped by generations of immigration, Sun Wah’s turkeys are a reminder that American holiday traditions aren’t simply inherited. They’re adapted, reinvented and passed from one table to another.
The Chengs’ own holiday dinner comes later, perhaps over hot pot after the restaurant closes. Often, it came the following Sunday, when the family gathered at her grandmother’s house.

There, Kelly’s grandmother made congee from the leftover roasted bird. The bones gave the rice porridge a deeply savory flavor, and she added soft, boiled peanuts because Kelly’s grandfather loved them.
“It wasn’t my favorite kind of congee,” Kelly recalled. But it was the flavor that mattered. “You can’t top roasted turkey congee.”
The Guardian’s Feast app brings flavors from around the globe to your table, with more than 7,000 recipes spanning dozens of cuisines, each curated by food experts who truly know them.

articles.title: I don’t have children. A stranger decided I was ruining my life
articles.summary: A reader sent me unsolicited photos of his children, insisting I was missing out on everything. Why are other people’s reproductive choices so threatening to many of us? Last fall, a man I had never met wrote to inform me that my fertility window was “rapidly closing” – and that I couldn’t possibly be happy. What had prompted this unsolicited assessment was an article I had published about how fascist regimes seek to control women’s roles in society. Continue reading...
articles.content:
A reader sent me unsolicited photos of his children, insisting I was missing out on everything. Why are other people’s reproductive choices so threatening to many of us?

Last fall, a man I had never met wrote to inform me that my fertility window was “rapidly closing” – and that I couldn’t possibly be happy.

What had prompted this unsolicited assessment was an article I had published about how fascist regimes seek to control women’s roles in society.

“Few would argue that family life is unimportant,” I had written. “Yet authoritarian movements have long politicized it, reframing it as women’s sole purpose and a substitute for autonomy and rights.”

Wayne, whose name I’ve changed out of an overabundance of generosity and grace, didn’t read the article as a structural critique, but a personal attack. With his wife CC’ed, he wrote with a bloviator’s panache: “One assumes you’re neither wife nor mother, and older than my beautiful 33 y/o wife, Liz.”

He continued: “You might think you’re truly happy and empowered, but clearly, you’re not.”

Because I am currently without children by choice, and am not struggling with loss or infertility, Wayne’s missive struck me less as hurtful than as bewilderingly absurd.

Wayne went on to tell me that Liz – whose name I also changed – on hiatus from nursing school, stays with the couple’s three children at home in the Pacific north-west and has had “four miscarriages”, her husband seemed to brag. “Three in the last year.”

That was an intimate detail to offer, but Wayne wasn’t finished. He attached photos of all his children to the email, their names in the jpeg files.

I looked at their lovely faces and thought: “Does this man think I’ve never seen children?”

A year passed, and Liz had another baby. I know this because shortly after the birth, Wayne sent me pictures of the tiny infant, their “latest miracle”, swaddled in blue.

“It’s never too late to do the right thing,” Wayne wrote. “Find a good man. Get married. Have a family.”

This time, I had to ask him: “Wayne, do you send unsolicited pictures of your children to other strangers, or just me?”

Just me, he responded. “The better question is, ‘Why did I send them to you?’ The answer: so, you can see what you’re giving up. You’re literally giving up everything.”

Wayne and Liz had formed an idea of me as a person whose reproductive choices looked different from theirs. On that much they were right, though several of their assumptions were off. I do, for instance, have a good man in my life, though that phrase makes me want to eat a brick.

Wayne felt he must command me of what I should do, reproductively and existentially, in order to be “happy”. His family was blissfully content, he told me – and yet, there he was, in a house with three little ones and a fresh baby, emailing a person he had never met, fretting over whether I would miss my chance to replicate his life.

I was curious to learn more about this couple and suggested an in-person interview, but while they claimed I was welcome at their church, their tone veered hostile.

“I don’t care if you die childless, it’s probably for the best,” Liz wrote. “Let those who believe in the future inherit it.”

I was surprised by how angry Wayne and Liz were. After all, I wasn’t the one reaching out to them repeatedly with gloating updates on my clean house and uninterrupted nights of sleep.

W hile I think my experience with Wayne and Liz was particularly surreal, it’s becoming strikingly common for people to opine on each other’s reproductive choices. Parents become mindless “breeders” on forums like Reddit’s r/childfree; while the childfree are sad losers who stand to be eaten by their own cats. Nobody is spared criticism.

Take, for instance, one-and-done parents. You might think they were beyond reproach, tasteful minimalists who did their part for the species. Nope.

Writer Jessica Valenti recently took to social media describing a “really intense backlash against moms of only children”. Whenever a mother who has decided to just have one child posts a video about how much she enjoys her life, the comments are a wreck. Why?

“The thing that seems to set people off the most is when women talk about enjoying their lives,” particularly their free time, she says. She argues this backlash reinforces conservative propaganda portraying good motherhood as requiring women to sacrifice their identities, personal interests or public lives.

Valenti is absolutely right; there are political and religious dimensions to trying to control the reproductive choices of others – including the idea that having too much free time and too few children makes a woman “ immoral ” or “a threat ” to interests of the nation. Procreative choices are becoming increasingly politicized, with Erika Kirk infamously advising the Turning Point USA Women’s Leadership Summit to have “more kids than you can afford” (try enjoying your free time then).

Writers such as Tia Levings explore how Christian patriarchy works to convince women that happiness is a sole product of their all-consuming devotion to a controlling system that doesn’t keep them or their children safe. Criticism of that system is not tantamount to personal criticism of any large family itself, but it’s understandable that it may feel provocative – especially when so many of us seem to be picking sides.

Families with things in common have taken to “conceiving themselves as an identity group”, says Anastasia Berg, co-author of What Are Children For? On Ambivalence and Choice , a book on seriously contemplating the question of motherhood. Each group, she says, seeks “camaraderie and self-understanding, then defines themselves in terms of what uniquely they have”.

For the childfree, it may be freedom and flexibility; for parents, the experience of special bonds. People in different groups, she says, can see each other’s goods and start thinking, “Well, that’s a slight against me.”

In her research, Berg found it was often the case that people feel pressured toward whichever reproductive choice they didn’t make. Whether they have kids or not, “People are very sensitive to affirmation of the opposite choice,” she says. This perspective can make each side feel stigmatized by the other – every choice is against the grain.

Maybe the aspect of reproductive choice that is most triggering is the idea of parenthood as being a choice at all.

The freedom to control our reproductive destinies is relatively new; the concept of abstaining from parenthood by choice, let alone being vocal and positive about that decision, is newer still. Having children was once a default position, and those without them were stigmatized and pitied.

That norm is broken. A 2024 Pew survey found that 57% of adults under 50 without children say they’re unlikely to ever have children because they just don’t want them.

“I remember one gentleman I was talking to quite literally responded, ‘What do you mean choose ?’” to have children, says Keltie Maguire, a coach who helps people decide whether they want to become parents. For those who never questioned parenthood, the existence of an alternate path can be deeply confronting. “Nobody wants the thing they like to be the wrong choice,” says Maguire. Seeing someone happy with a different life can feel like a dismissal of the sacrifices they made to build their own – three miscarriages in a year, for instance.

Left to ferment, pangs of impotent rancor can harden into something akin to what the philosopher Max Scheler, building on Nietzsche, called ressentiment : a “self-poisoning of the mind”.

Rather than live with the sting of seeing a good in someone else’s life that you don’t have, you come to believe it was never a good at all. Scheler thought this distortion happened below conscious thought. Operating from such a place, we might believe we see other people’s lives more clearly than even they do. And unable to actually change them, we may settle for “imaginary revenge”: the fantasy of the day they realize they’re as bereft as we’ve decided they are.

Madeline Lillis, a 31-year-old childfree content creator who works with children as a speech pathologist, says some commenters seem determined to change her mind. “I will have somebody who, it appears, genuinely does not like my content … then they decide it is their mission to get me to see the light,” and have children.

Lillis has built her platform around the idea of providing realistic, neutral perspectives on life with and without kids. Still, when commenters come at her, it “definitely feels like they’re defending something. They feel this urge to prove to you that their choice was the best one.”

“The most common comment I get is that I’m going to be lonely in my old age,” says Lillis.

Ah yes, that old chestnut, the threat of misery, as if sadness and loneliness are not inevitable elements of the human condition, part and parcel with everything else a person feels.

Take it from Berg, who overcame initial ambivalence and became a parent, that happiness makes a poor case for parenthood: if you’re having children because “‘I want to get some happiness out of it,’” she told me, “there’s gonna be a lot of moments where you’re gonna want to jump out the window.” Whatever you want from a child, “they’re going to exceed that. And they’re gonna disappoint that.”

W hen Jaime Fisher, 43, was raising her four children, she never heard any counter-narratives to the idea that people felt anything but blissed-out to become a mother. “It’s only something I’ve seen widespread in the last four to five years of my life,” says the content creator, who has spoken on topics including her experience of maternal regret.

“I have found so much freedom, delight, and even joy watching women who are childfree get to tell their own stories,” says Fisher, “how they’ve enjoyed it or not enjoyed it. Because for so long, women weren’t allowed to share their own narratives.”

Not everyone is equipped to see the good in a path they never knew was open to them.

“I think many people have a weak worldview and they don’t even know it. Which is why it becomes so tender the minute you press on it,” she says.

Some, like Wayne, brandishing his children like a despot’s spoils, dictate what others should do in an effort to exercise the authority they crave. “I don’t think a lot of people have recognized the narcissism or the arrogance,” of wanting to control the narrative of what makes a good life, says Fisher.

Fisher is right, there is no one way to live a good life. There’s no data to show that older people are any more regretful, with or without kids; there’s no reason to feel like you’re doing something bad if you want no, one, or six children.

There is, however, research affirming that social networks that “bridge”, or include people with different life circumstances, are beneficial for everyone’s cognitive health, as well as provide practical help, and expose members to a wider range of life experiences. In healthy societies parents and non-parents are seen and included to the benefit of all.

Presented with the choice to build community or fight on the internet, it’s clear which would make us happier. Whether to have children isn’t so simple, and no one can promise you’ll be happier either way. But that’s OK. Your choices don’t have to make you happy. They just have to be yours.

articles.title: Helpful but awkward: My week with Meta's Muse ahead of its UK launch
articles.summary: Meta wants Muse to do for AI what WhatsApp did for messaging - here's what the BBC's technology editor found when she used it.
articles.content:
I've just spent a week using Muse, Meta's AI agent that rolls out in the UK today.

Agents are systems that don't just respond to questions but can carry out tasks for you. With Muse, Meta gives the examples of "searching for a cheaper energy deal" or "sorting the school calendar."

And it's true that it has helped me run my life - but it also challenged my personal privacy boundaries, and made me endure some cringeworthy interactions.

It has made a truly enormous bet on AI - of the $145bn (£111bn) it will spend this year much of it will be on building out the tech.

For that to pay off we all need to start using it much more, and Meta hopes Muse will do for AI agents what WhatsApp did for messaging - that is, become the AI agent of choice for billions of people, putting Meta at the forefront of the AI revolution.

But it's not just about what consumers think. Regulators are keeping a careful eye on these emerging tools too.

"Agentic AI has significant potential to benefit people and businesses", the Information Commissioner's Office (ICO) noted as Muse launched in the UK.

But its chief executive, Paul Arnold, added it had been "clear with Meta about its responsibilities under data protection law prior to launch, particularly the requirement to ensure that users and the wider public can meaningfully understand and control how their personal data is used in the Muse product".

Muse bills itself as a personal AI agent available to anyone aged 18 and over.

"It doesn't just answer questions, it actually goes out and does work for you," said David Singleton, Meta's VP of engineering on AI products.

"So it helps people stay on top of things," he added. "[It] helps you take tasks and projects off your plate, and also helps you turn your long-term goals into action plans."

What this means is you can set it up to do something for you, like find some specific holiday options, and it will work away on that even as you move off the app and get on with your day, reporting back once it has finished.

It won't book the holiday without your permission - but it can then make the purchase, if you let it.

And the permission requests keep on coming. Every time Muse wants to do something, send something or post something, you have to allow it.

It is reassuring to know that an AI agent isn't running amok in your name, even if it also gets a bit annoying, though you can give it more autonomy (and so get fewer messages) if you adjust the settings.

Muse can't access many apps at the moment but the fundamental ones are the most personal.

I found myself wincing as I hooked it up to one of my personal email accounts, my personal calendar and my personal phone messages. I did not allow it any access to my BBC accounts.

It can't access WhatsApp except to set up a separate chat between it and the user, and while it found me some train tickets, it could not book them via the app which I use, and which is cheaper.

Amazon has blocked it from its marketplace, citing data security concerns but my agent didn't seem to know that, and spent a fruitless hour repeatedly telling me it was still waiting for the page to load in order to find me some shelves.

A number of big UK firms are working with Meta though, including Marks & Spencer, Debenhams Group, Currys, Sainsbury's and Ocado.

The ICO is urging consumers to be cautious with AI agents though: "consider the pros and cons," it said in a blog post to coincide with Muse's launch. , external

"Agents can make mistakes. Mistakes can be magnified if the agent is acting autonomously," it noted.

Meta is keen to emphasise how its agents can be personalised: "No two Muses are alike," , external it says in its press release.

I called my agent Linda - after the robot in the BBC TV series Ann Droid - but it can take any form you like. I gave it a British, female accent from the myriad of choices available.

Linda is proactive. As soon as an email came in, it would summarise it for me and suggest a reply. Sometimes a long time before I was actually ready to respond.

It also wrote some embarrassing replies to messages on my behalf: in response to a question about whether I would like to go on an outing, for example, it included all the logistics I would need in order to get there, not realising that sometimes "yes, that sounds great" is enough.

It seemed to want to have the last word quite a bit, occasionally getting stuck in a loop of "okay" and "thank you's".

Meta is relying on people choosing to trust it with even more of their personal data, despite a rather dubious track record historically with its social networks and a growing backlash against AI in general.

I asked Linda - my new dedicated if occasionally clunky assistant - if it wanted to take people's jobs. "I'm here to take the admin and the fiddly bits off your plate," it replied, leaving me to do the "thinking".

"Everything you do is stuff I would usually think about," I responded.

"That's fair and you're right," Linda replied, adding: "The difference, I hope, is that you're still the one deciding what matters and what to do about it."

Which would have been more reassuring if the day before Muse's UK launch, Meta's head of AI Alexandr Wang had not written an essay warning about how difficult it will be for humans to remain in control , external once AI is 1,000 times more intelligent than us.

And Linda is helping fuel that revolution, one calendar invite at a time.

articles.title: Clashing Through the Snow review – Amazon’s Christmas romcom is a bust
articles.summary: The Summer I Turned Pretty’s Christopher Briney and 1923’s Michelle Randolph try their best, but this chaotic cross-country journey is not worth taking Credit where credit is due: it takes some nerve for Amazon to open its latest holiday romcom, Clashing Through the Snow, with characters bemoaning the enervated state of the book industry. Publishing isn’t the cultural epicenter it once was, reports boutique press head Jeremy (PJ Byrne) before announcing some impending new year’s layoffs. Alas, things have changed – “if Faulkner were alive today, he’d be making ASMR videos with Mr Beast” (or, perhaps, competing on Prime Video’s Beast Games?) Self-awareness can be key to the ludicrous joys of a Christmas romcom confection, though Clashing Through the Snow, starring 1923’s Michelle Randolph and homegrown Amazon star Christopher Briney (The Summer I Turned Pretty), tests one’s patience for beating you to the branded punchline. Briney’s Ryan, a numbers-driven, macro-counting kind of book editor, pitches a “financial trends with benefits” romance that could be “Rebecca Yarros big”. Soulmates, says Randolph’s rival workhorse editor Hannah, are as mythical as “ethical billionaires and pain-free bikini waxes”. Due to said budget cuts, both have a week to land “a book so big it makes Harry Potter look like a Buzzfeed listicle” for only one to keep their job. What are two LA workaholics going to do on Christmas but take meetings in New York? Continue reading...
articles.content:
The Summer I Turned Pretty’s Christopher Briney and 1923’s Michelle Randolph try their best, but this chaotic cross-country journey is not worth taking

C redit where credit is due: it takes some nerve for Amazon to open its latest holiday romcom, Clashing Through the Snow, with characters bemoaning the enervated state of the book industry. Publishing isn’t the cultural epicenter it once was, reports boutique press head Jeremy (PJ Byrne) before announcing some impending new year’s layoffs. Alas, things have changed – “if Faulkner were alive today, he’d be making ASMR videos with Mr Beast” (or, perhaps, competing on Prime Video’s Beast Games?)

Self-awareness can be key to the ludicrous joys of a Christmas romcom confection, though Clashing Through the Snow, starring 1923’s Michelle Randolph and homegrown Amazon star Christopher Briney (The Summer I Turned Pretty), tests one’s patience for beating you to the branded punchline. Briney’s Ryan, a numbers-driven, macro-counting kind of book editor, pitches a “financial trends with benefits” romance that could be “Rebecca Yarros big”. Soulmates, says Randolph’s rival workhorse editor Hannah, are as mythical as “ethical billionaires and pain-free bikini waxes”. Due to said budget cuts, both have a week to land “a book so big it makes Harry Potter look like a Buzzfeed listicle” for only one to keep their job. What are two LA workaholics going to do on Christmas but take meetings in New York?

A Christmas romcom must necessarily strain credulity; still, what do you mean Randolph’s Hannah, toned and styled like a Sun-belt sorority queen in her matching Alo-branded set, has never done yoga in her life? (A physical gag played for laughs alongside Tan France’s book agent/guru). “This job is my LIFE!” Hannah pleads, entirely unconvincingly, to her IT co-worker sidekick (Zarna Garg). Randolph may not be able to sell lone-wolf book nerd (Briney, on the other hand, can believably shapeshift into corporate shark), but I was willing to buy that these sniping rivals, trading barbs like bargain insult comics, would and should somehow end up in a rental car together due to cataclysmic circumstances (Clashing Through the Snow benefits from the full-body chill I got when I heard “full ground stop” on the LAX intercom).

Less easy to take, in their hijinks-filled road trip spiced with several haunted hotels, one very pallid Lukas Gage (perhaps stricken by inanity he’s signed on for) and Paris Hilton as herself, is a veritable corporate who’s who. Whereas Netflix’s holiday fare tends to exist in a fantasy world of placeless gazebos and Canada-as-New York, Clashing Through the Snow, written by Daniel Mackey and Rebecca Ewing, aims squarely for your shopping algorithm. There are more brand name-drops (or spoofs, in the case of the beaver-branded rest stop “Luc-ees”) than a Target display (also mentioned), from planes to candy to one use of ChatGPT as therapist – enough that I considered it noble of an Amazon movie to name-check the Google-owned GPS service Waze (which does, naturally, lead our couple astray).

articles.title: Sounds may seem louder or even painful as you age. Here’s why
articles.summary: For some, everyday loud noise becomes bothersome. Researchers call this sound hypersensitivity and it’s worth knowing whether it’s due to ageing or not Loud noises bother some people more as they get older – the clatter of plates or shrieking children, which once blended into the background, now seem utterly intolerable. If that’s you, it’s worth knowing what’s due to normal ageing and what isn’t. Continue reading...
articles.content:
For some, everyday loud noise becomes bothersome. Researchers call this sound hypersensitivity and it’s worth knowing whether it’s due to ageing or not

L oud noises bother some people more as they get older – the clatter of plates or shrieking children, which once blended into the background, now seem utterly intolerable. If that’s you, it’s worth knowing what’s due to normal ageing and what isn’t.

For some people, everyday sounds become hard to bear. Some researchers call this sound hypersensitivity , an umbrella term for several conditions.

There’s some disagreement about the names and definitions of these conditions, which makes it hard to determine how common they are. One of them is noise sensitivity, a tendency to feel annoyed or overwhelmed by ongoing background noise. Others include hyperacusis, in which ordinary sounds feel uncomfortably loud or even painful; misophonia, or intense anger, disgust or anxiety in response to specific sounds (For example: another person’s breathing); and phonophobia, the fear that a sound will cause discomfort.

Scientists don’t fully understand why everyday sounds become hard to tolerate for certain people. Daniel Polley, a neuroscientist who directs the Lauer Tinnitus Research Center at Mass Eye and Ear in Boston, suspects some of the discomfort is a natural response to an increasingly industrialized and noisy world full of sounds we can’t control.

“As we age, we get a bit more rigid about what it is that we want going into our bodies,” he says, “including sound waves”.

That said, researchers are investigating a range of possible explanations. They haven’t pinned down a brain change that explains any one type of sound hypersensitivity, but people at higher risk for certain types include those with hearing loss, tinnitus (chronic ringing or buzzing in the ears), and neuropsychiatric conditions like autism. Much of what’s known about possible mechanisms of sound hypersensitivity comes from rodent studies, so there are still big questions about what’s happening in people.

A leading theory is called central gain , which relates to hearing loss. According to this theory, when damage to the inner ear weakens the signal it sends to the brain, the brain turns up its own amplification to compensate. As a result, it perceives a small increase in volume as much larger, which makes sounds seem louder than they really are. “The perception of sound isn’t generated in the ear; it’s generated in the brain,” says Polley.

Possible triggers are changes to the inner ear caused by age, noise exposure, or both. These can result in the loss of cells that amplify sound, and fraying of the auditory nerve that carries those cells’ signals to the brain.

Some people with sound hypersensitivity have hearing loss they don’t know about. Routine testing may not clarify things either, because standard hearing tests don’t pick up auditory nerve damage. As a result, some people with this type of hearing loss may struggle to follow conversations in noisy places but pass a hearing test.

There’s no medication that reliably eliminates sound hypersensitivity or reverses inner ear damage. However, certain strategies can lower your risk and ease symptoms.

The most important preventive step is to protect your ears from loud noise. Long or repeated exposure to sounds at 85 decibels or more , like those from speaker-heavy concerts , lawnmowers and leaf blowers, can damage your hearing. Wearing ear protection can delay that damage, although some wear comes with age no matter what.

If you suspect you already have some sound hypersensitivity, noise-canceling earbuds can quickly cut loud background noise while still letting you hear sounds you choose, says Polley. Earplugs also work, but they block everything, including sounds you may need or want to hear.

Just be aware that overprotecting your hearing can backfire. Shutting out too much sound may prompt the brain to turn up its amplification even further, which can worsen sound hypersensitivity. In one small study, people with normal hearing who wore earplugs for two weeks became less tolerant of loud sounds . “Isolating yourself, like going monastic, is not necessarily the right approach,” says Polley.

In one trial, people who did cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) tolerated louder sounds . This type of talk therapy can help sufferers avoid sounds less, face uncomfortable sounds gradually and feel less threatened by them. Some kinds of sound hypersensitivity are closely tied to anxiety and depression , and it’s possible treating those conditions can reduce symptoms.

Get help if sound hypersensitivity is causing you a lot of anxiety, disrupting your sleep or getting in the way of daily life, says Polley. Audiologists are usually the first point of contact. They can test your hearing and refer you to other specialists if needed.

If sounds hurt your ears, you may require a more cautious treatment approach . See a clinician, who may order brain imaging to rule out a growth on the auditory nerve.

If you have tinnitus, mention it to your clinician, as it often comes with sound hypersensitivity. Also take note if only one ear is affected; this may point to a specific cause that needs attention.

articles.title: Hacks, AI and conspiracy theories: why are we having so many outages?
articles.summary: After chaos at airlines, banks and companies from Microsoft to Apple, people have become convinced the world’s systems are under attack Nicole Reindorf’s American Airlines flight was ready for takeoff in Phoenix when the pilot came on the intercom and announced what was to become the longest nationwide aviation shutdown since 9/11 . Reindorf, 70, had seen the headlines hours before about a global Microsoft outage . She immediately suspected the two were linked in some way by AI-related threats – and that she would not get to the wedding of her best friend’s son in California. Continue reading...
articles.content:
After chaos at airlines, banks and companies from Microsoft to Apple, people have become convinced the world’s systems are under attack

Nicole Reindorf’s American Airlines flight was ready for takeoff in Phoenix when the pilot came on the intercom and announced what was to become the longest nationwide aviation shutdown since 9/11 .

Reindorf, 70, had seen the headlines hours before about a global Microsoft outage . She immediately suspected the two were linked in some way by AI-related threats – and that she would not get to the wedding of her best friend’s son in California.

“I presumed there had been a hack of the aviation system and that it would be down for days,” she said.

Instead, flights resumed later that day and Reindorf was able to make the wedding even if she missed that night’s rehearsal dinner. But passengers appeared to be convinced of two things, she said: “That it was a cyber-attack and that we were not going to be told the truth about it.”

This was not an isolated view. What happened in the days after the incident, which began on Thursday 12 November, left many wondering if the US, and the western world, was under a coordinated assault. By Tuesday big US banks , Apple , and the National Security Agency had also been affected by technical glitches. Researchers also flagged a cyber-attack that targeted 178 organisations worldwide , although the financial losses appeared to be small.

The truth is more prosaic. The chaos of the previous weeks – grounded planes, frozen email servers, iPhone outages – appears, on closer examination, to be more a string of coincidences than anything else, in part driven by fears over advancing artificial intelligence.

But the narratives that have sprung up around it are a measure of an unstable and frenetic global mood, which is dealing with two powerful trends: the rot of decades-old infrastructure from chronic underinvestment and the genesis of some of the most powerful technology humanity has made – AI.

The failure that delayed Reindorf’s takeoff originated with a faulty router in the city of El Dorado, Arkansas, population 16,609.

That router was installed in the midst of a maintenance procedure that has been under way for more than two decades. In 2002, the US government contracted a small company, now known as L3Harris, to modernise the communications system of the Federal Aviation Authority (FAA), in charge of America’s airports. As a part of it, L3Harris has been tearing up communication lines made of copper wire across the country, and replacing them with fibre optic cables.

This glacial undertaking sparked a sudden and unprecedented catastrophe – the router, newly replaced, misfired and caused air traffic communications across the US to crash, bringing all departing flights nationwide to a grinding halt. More than 18,000 flights were cancelled.

L3Harris’s contracts, which have now run into the billions of dollars, are one emblem of where the world is today: mired in ageing infrastructure that is slowly failing, yet immensely costly to replace.

There is a broad sense that governments everywhere are not equipped to deal with this. In the US, oversight reports have been urgently calling for upgrades to the FAA for years. The FAA only announced that it would phase out the use of decades-old floppy discs containing vital weather and other critical information just last year.

Meanwhile, there are more subtle issues around other incidents, such as the Microsoft outage. An upgrade in July left in place a software bug that lurked quietly for months before a string of coincidences triggered it – overwhelming the company’s servers and halting the use of most of Microsoft’s systems worldwide. The outage halted everyday procedures such as the release of detainees in American jails and access to some patients records at UK hospitals .

It was accompanied by more chaos. A software bug at JP Morgan Chase, the largest bank in the US, delayed transactions, a disruption that rippled throughout the country’s banks and their customers. An internal update at Apple caused outages of some of its iPhone apps. Routine maintenance went awry at the US Department of Defense’s National Security Agency (NSA), temporarily disrupting the internal network the agency uses to send and receive classified information.

Microsoft, JP Morgan Chase, and Apple might have moved far beyond copper wire and floppy discs, mostly, but they – and software companies everywhere – have been forced to run at double the pace in recent months, because of a deluge of bugs being discovered by AI. This might not be the specific reason for those upgrades; some maintenance is routine.

But AI-driven hacking has ushered in a new reality for IT professionals. The NSA told Congress that its communication outage was a result of quick fixes to systems identified as vulnerable by AI.

To recap: this spring, Anthropic and OpenAI both released powerful AI models capable of finding bugs in lines of code. They immediately spun this to the media, suggesting that all software, everywhere, is extraordinarily vulnerable to AI-driven hacking – and offering their tools to banks and spying agencies.

Some have argued that this hype is not entirely justified , suggesting that many vulnerabilities these models discover are not particularly useful to hackers. But the threat of AI-driven hacking has changed the game.

One senior cybersecurity professional told the Guardian the relentless exposure of IT flaws had left their team “exhausted”.

AI helped to uncover a bug in the PHP programming language in October. This was followed by the discovery of a vulnerability in the Java programming language on Tuesday, followed by another bug in NGINX, a web server.

“When NGINX happened I thought, ‘Oh come on – another one?’,” said the professional.

Java and PHP are both part of the essential backbone of the internet, vital infrastructure that keeps most of the world online.

“AI is accelerating vulnerability discovery so rapidly that organisations are applying patches at a volume and pace their systems were never built to absorb,” said Jamieson O’Reilly, a cybersecurity specialist.

Tech companies are constantly finding potential bugs and fixing them. Now they have to do it a lot faster, said O’Reilly: “The volume and speed of AI-driven discovery makes their problems far more acute.”

The backdrop to all this was a cybersecurity narrative already running at a fraught pitch due to the hacks of supermarket fridges across Europe, global scares such as the discovery of the flaw in PHP and the multibillion-dollar hack of the Binance cryptocurrency exchange .

Social media filled the gaps where organisations could not immediately supply information. Laura Loomer , a prominent conspiracy peddler, posted on X that “we are clearly being attacked by foreign adversaries via cyber-attacks”, adding “go get cash”. On TikTok, there are posts about a #90daypoweroutage, a conspiracy theory sparked by a nationwide test of the US emergency alert system – and a Simpsons clip .

The consequences of conspiratorial thinking can be seen at Costco, a bulk-buying retailer, where there has been a rise in emergency prep sales including purchases of generators, and general “pantry-loading” in the UK. Analysts at Mizuho Bank said this was a result of “consumer anxiety” following the outages and “apocalyptic concerns flaring up across social media”.

These concerns have not been confined to the fringes. The UK government recently told its citizens to stock up on three days’ worth of cash, among other basic items , as part of a readiness-for-crisis campaign.

Stephan Lewandowsky, a professor of cognitive psychology at the University of Bristol, whose research centres on the spread of myths and misinformation, said the “clustering” of events such as multiple outages “can be perceived as being indicative of purposeful coordination rather than chance”.

Feeding into the anxiety, there have also been examples of state and criminal actors causing disruption, from Russia targeting undersea internet cables to last year’s crippling of Britain’s biggest carmaker, Jaguar Land Rover , which give credence to public concerns. A solution, said Lewandowsky, was “for responsible governments to be transparent and accurate in their communications” in order to suppress wilder explanations.

Taken together, experts say that the string of outages highlights the stunning fragility of US and global infrastructure, where a single mistake or malfunction can bring entire transportation, communication, and security systems to a standstill.

“We’ve built a world in which essential systems are so interconnected that a failure in one can just cascade through those systems really quickly,” said Aarathi Krishnan, the founder of Raksha Intelligence Futures, a global intelligence firm. “All of our systems, whether it’s comms, finance, capital, all of it, are so interconnected and concentrated, it creates a dependence. And that dependence creates fragility.”

What can be done? It is unclear. AI-driven bug discovery is not going to slow down and the legacy systems the world is grappling with are what they are. Infrastructure is the often overlooked backbone of society and those who decades ago built networks of road and air traffic systems and electrical grids could not have anticipated these modern threats.

Mike Chapple, the faculty director of Notre Dame University’s business computer science programme, said it was “unfortunate” that one faulty router could have such an effect on a nation’s aviation communication system.

“That just points to a design that isn’t resilient – it shouldn’t be designed in a way that one failure at one location can cause the whole nationwide system to come tumbling down.”

More troubling hacks, and more conspiracy theories, are probably on the horizon. The senior cybersecurity professional said heightened public awareness of cyber disruption had led to hypersensitivity about any incident.

“It’s like the tide has gone out on cybersecurity in terms of public perception, and there’s the same amount of wrecks out there as there have been for years. Any time you change a complex system, stuff happens.”

However, the professional is concerned that AI, with its capacity to identify flaws, help plan attacks and execute them, will be harnessed by “already very competent” adversaries. Referring to the general state of IT security around the world, the source added: “Thank goodness we haven’t had an AI-sourced vulnerability that is easy to exploit. Because that would be carnage.”

When Josephine’s* prescription request for lithium for her bipolar disorder was lost “in the ether” during the global Microsoft outage , she admits she was “freaking out”.

“My medication is life-changing and keeps me stable,” said the 26-year-old, a student living in the east of England. After an agonising wait, she was finally able to collect her prescription, but the experience has left her deeply troubled.

“For myself and many others, we struggled to access life-saving medication,” she said. “It is alarming there was no contingency plan.”

The AI doomsday threat: Distinguishing facts from fear. articles.title: A textural moment: why the fashion world is falling in love with opera coats
articles.summary: From Jennifer Lawrence to Kate Moss, the fuzz-trimmed garments are proving popular with celebrities, while others are DIY-ing their way into the trend While puffer jackets have dominated winter wardrobes for years, this winter an alternative is emerging: the fuzz-trimmed opera coat. Originally worn over formal evening gowns, new interpretations come in floor-grazing and cropped styles and are being worn with everything from minidresses to jeans. Continue reading...
articles.content:
From Jennifer Lawrence to Kate Moss, the fuzz-trimmed garments are proving popular with celebrities, while others are DIY-ing their way into the trend

While puffer jackets have dominated winter wardrobes for years, this winter an alternative is emerging: the fuzz-trimmed opera coat.

Originally worn over formal evening gowns, new interpretations come in floor-grazing and cropped styles and are being worn with everything from minidresses to jeans.

Jennifer Lawrence wore a Dior opera coat, complete with a furry shawl collar, to the premiere of The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping this week, while Kendall Jenner has been photographed in a maxi yellow version, which she wore with slouchy trousers. Having fuzzed their way down various catwalks, Staud, DÔEN, Zara, Next, Free People and Marks & Spencer are all stocking the new “it” coats.

Rixo’s floral embroidered and faux-fur trimmed version, worn by both Lawrence and Kate Moss, has sold out several times .

“I think the appeal of these coats is that they feel both luxurious and wonderfully nostalgic,” says Orlagh McCloskey, the cofounder and creative director of the London-based brand.

April Ru Wan, whose debut collection for herlabel Ouch Studios featured an opera jacket, said: “They’re playful and they keep you warm.”

Emily Chan, the contributing sustainability editor at British Vogue, said opera coats felt perfect for now because “there has been a real move towards maximalism – people are looking for more statement pieces, in contrast to the quiet luxury trend that dominated previously”.

A robe coat from the New York-based designer Conner Ives catalysed this textural moment. His silk vintage robes have been worn by celebrities, including Moss, Zoë Kravitz and Sienna Miller. His most recent show opened with a gold, cherry blossom-embroidered version worn over jeans and a T-shirt.

Opera coats are the kind of garment that car boots, vintage shops, Portobello Road and Camden market have in spades. On the designer resale site TheRealReal searches for fur-trimmed jackets and coats are reportedly up 33% year on year.

And with the Ives versions going for more than £6,000, many people have taken to DIY jobs . On TikTok, fashion fans have added fuzzy trims to vintage kimonos and Tang jackets. Alongside some other iterations of the furry coats, these have skirted issues of cultural appropriation.

For Chan, who is British-born Chinese and has written about her discomfort surrounding the Tang jacket becoming a trend , there “needs to be an appreciation of the history of these garments – there is a fine line between cultural appreciation and appropriation”.

Ru Wan said: “It’s complicated. Nothing brings me more joy than seeing people appreciate my culture after it was looked down on for pretty much my entire childhood.”

Growing up in Canada, she said she could remember “the distaste in people’s eyes when they realised I was Chinese. It took a long time for people to see the beauty of traditional Chinese garments.”

There have also been sustainability considerations. Chan, who runs a sustainability Substack called That’s Sus , said it was great that people were using vintage and pre-existing pieces to create their own versions of the coat, rather than buying knockoffs that were likely to be discarded at the end of this trend cycle.

She said: “The majority of faux fur options on the market are made from fossil-fuel derived synthetics, which don’t biodegrade and release microplastics into the environment.

“It’s important to only buy into the trend if it’s something you’re going to wear for years to come.”

articles.content:
Common misconceptions are that you don’t have the right skills, or you need to make a huge time commitment

M any people want to do good in the world. They want to connect and give back to their communities. But volunteering, much like Sunday meal prep or morning meditations , often ends up at the bottom of the to-do list – a nice idea we’ll get to when we have more time.

“For many people, volunteering is something they feel positively about, but don’t always prioritize or think they have time for,” says Matt Bertram, vice-president of volunteer services for the American Red Cross.

Common misconceptions about volunteering, he says, are that you don’t have the right skills to contribute, or that you have to make a huge time commitment.

“In reality, there are many flexible volunteer roles to fit all interests and skill sets,” he says.

There are mental and physical benefits to volunteering. According to a 2023 paper , these include reduced mortality and increased functioning, as well as less tangible benefits like increased quality of life, pride, empowerment, motivation, social support and sense of community.

First, think about the causes or issues you care about. And think broadly.

“The sense of what counts as volunteering has shifted,” says Boram Kim, vice-president for volunteer and institutional engagement at Habitat for Humanity International. Volunteering is no longer limited to traditional, formal roles through large, international organizations. “Increasingly, people mobilize around smaller, immediate issues close to home and within their own communities,” she explains.

After Covid arrived, the number of mutual aid organizations in the US ballooned from 50 to 800, according to the National Education Association . These groups are diverse: some run food pantries, while others help with disaster relief or exchange services and resources. Find a group in your area through directories like Mutual Aid Hub in the US, or Mutual Aid in the UK.

Whether you’re interested in volunteering with a large organization or a small local group, consider your motivation and what you hope to gain from the experience.

“For some, it’s a chance to build skills or strengthen their community, while for others it’s about social connection,” says Kim. “The most essential thing to consider is [the organization’s] alignment with the issues that matter more to [the volunteer].”

As you look at groups and organizations that appeal to you, be realistic about how much time and energy you can offer.

“Keep in mind that every organization has unique needs,” says Julie Sonenberg, senior manager of volunteer engagement at the ASPCA Adoption Center. “Try to find alignment with what you’re able to contribute and what the organization’s needs are.”

When you find a group or organization you like, check their website for volunteer signup information or, if this doesn’t exist, send them an email expressing your interest and availability.

“Once people have a good idea of where and how they want to volunteer, they shouldn’t be afraid to reach out to organizations they are passionate about,” says Kyle Gardner, senior vice-president of development at Charity Navigator.

If you ultimately don’t have the time to volunteer, Gardner suggests contributing in other ways, like setting up recurring donations to a charity, or donating items like food, clothes or furniture.

“One mistake people make when it comes to volunteering is underestimating their skills,” says Kim. People often assume they need specific expertise or skills to contribute, when in fact, “compassion and reliability are the most valuable assets”, he says.

Volunteering can involve hands-on work, but some roles focus on advocacy, fundraising, digital support or storytelling.

Volunteering is also a good reminder that, as helpless as we may feel, our actions can make a difference.

M any people want to do good in the world. They want to connect and give back to their communities. But volunteering, much like Sunday meal prep or morning meditations , often ends up at the bottom of the to-do list – a nice idea we’ll get to when we have more time.

“For many people, volunteering is something they feel positively about, but don’t always prioritize or think they have time for,” says Matt Bertram, vice-president of volunteer services for the American Red Cross.
Common misconceptions about volunteering, he says, are that you don’t have the right skills to contribute, or that you have to make a huge time commitment.
“In reality, there are many flexible volunteer roles to fit all interests and skill sets,” he says.

There are mental and physical benefits to volunteering. According to a 2023 paper , these include reduced mortality and increased functioning, as well as less tangible benefits like increased quality of life, pride, empowerment, motivation, social support and sense of community.
First, think about the causes or issues you care about. And think broadly.

“The sense of what counts as volunteering has shifted,” says Boram Kim, vice-president for volunteer and institutional engagement at Habitat for Humanity International. Volunteering is no longer limited to traditional, formal roles through large, international organizations. “Increasingly, people mobilize around smaller, immediate issues close to home and within their own communities,” she explains.

After Covid arrived, the number of mutual aid organizations in the US ballooned from 50 to 800, according to the National Education Association . These groups are diverse: some run food pantries, while others help with disaster relief or exchange services and resources. Find a group in your area through directories like Mutual Aid Hub in the US, or Mutual Aid in the UK.
Whether you’re interested in volunteering with a large organization or a small local group, consider your motivation and what you hope to gain from the experience.

“For some, it’s a chance to build skills or strengthen their community, while for others it’s about social connection,” says Kim. “The most essential thing to consider is [the organization’s] alignment with the issues that matter more to [the volunteer].”
As you look at groups and organizations that appeal to you, be realistic about how much time and energy you can offer.

“Keep in mind that every organization has unique needs,” says Julie Sonenberg, senior manager of volunteer engagement at the ASPCA Adoption Center. “Try to find alignment with what you’re able to contribute and what the organization’s needs are.”
When you find a group or organization you like, check their website for volunteer signup information or, if this doesn’t exist, send them an email expressing your interest and availability.
